speechtext: Report of the Department of the Interior for the year ended March 31, 1914, volume I.-Mr. Roche.
On the Orders of the Day being called:

I have seen
a statement in the press to the effect that a steamship service has been inaugurated between France and Canada. Can the Minister of Trade and Commerce give us any information on that subject?
Sir GEO. FOSTER (Minister of Trade and Commerce): We have been informed that arrangements have been perfected by the British Admiralty by which eighteen vessels will be placed upon the service between our ports and Havre, France. The purpose of these vessels is to transport Government supplies, solely and entirely. It is calculated -and so far as I have seen the calculations, I think they bear out the basis on which they are made-that Government supplies

and requirements will tax the total capacity of these vessels. There will be a tri-weekly service. That is the general plan, but all the details have not yet been worked out. If it happens that any one of these vessels is not filled to capacity by the supplies being sent to the British or French Governments, then other Government supplies furnished by private or company contractors may be transported. The service, however, is not meant for general trade.
Do I understand that there is no correspondence on this subject?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
There is some
correspondence, but we are expecting further correspondence on the subject. As soon as the correspondence is complete, it will be brought down. In the latter part of January the Government sent a representative to Great Britain for the purpose of conferring with the War Office and with the Admiralty, in order that some provision might be made for the transport across the Atlantic of supplies purchased in Canada by the British or the French Government. It was observed at that time that tonnage was becoming extremely scarce, and rates abnormally high. Mr. A. H. Harris, of the Canadian Pacific Railway, who went to England for this purpose, has just returned; and we are informed by him that, as stated by my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce, eighteen vessels have been assigned by the British Admiralty to this service, and withdrawn from other service. We are informed that the vessels will be available for this purpose from now until the end of the war.
I understand that one or more vessels have already arrived on this side, and that one has been loaded and is now on her way back to Great Britain or France. Another advantage which will be of general interest is that, by this arrangement, the tonnage which has been used in carrying coal from Great Britain to Halifax for the use of the Admiralty at that port, and which has been heretofore used to a very considerable extent for the transport of these supplies, will, it is hoped, be available for general purposes, and in that way assist in supplying the general demands for tonnage to transport goods from Canada to the Mother Country.
What is the sailing port from Canada?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
No definite sailing port has been fixed. I presume that the boats will sail from St. John or Halifax in

the winter, and, when navigation opens on the St. Lawrence, that all or the greater part oi the tonnage will go by the St. Lawrence route. If it should appear that the necessities of transportation might be more advantageously met by the vessels sailing from ports in the maritime provinces, those ports would be available, and I have no doubt that suitable arrangements might be made to that effect with the British Admiralty. UNITED STATES POTATO EMBARGO. On the Orders of the Day being called:

I should
like to call the attention of the Acting Minister of Agriculture to a report I saw in the press a few days ago. It is headed " Canadian Potato is Under the Ban-United States Inspector's Report-Powder Scab Found," and reads as follows:
Hon. Martin Burrell, Minister of Agriculture, in December last made an arrangement with the Department of Agriculture at Washington, by which permits were to be issued to shippers of Canadian potatoes allowing potatoes to enter the United States. This arrangement was to continue so long as there was no powdery scab found in any of the shipments. Unfortunately the United States inspectors have reported that they have found powdery scab in a shipment of potatoes from New Brunswick to Boston and have given notice to the Department of Agriculture that no Canadian potatoes will be permitted to enter the United States from Canada after the 5th of March, instant. The potatoes complained of in Boston were immediately purchased for export from Boston and there was no difficulty, in so far as the quality was concerned, with the country to which they were to be exported. The Department of Agriculture is investigating to ascertain if the statements made by the United States inspectors have any foundation.
I should like to ask whether these are the facts; whether the department has made.an investigation, and whether potatoes can be shipped from Canada to the United States at the present time.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. D. REID (Minister of Customs):
speechtext:
The statement is correct. The Department of Agriculture has been notified by the United States authorities, as intimated in that despatch. A carload of potatoes shipped to Boston was condemned by the United States inspectors. Some hon. gentleman considered the potatoes all right, and purchased and shipped them to Cuba. The Department of Agriculture, feeling that the American inspectors were not justified in condemning the potatoes, sent an inspector to Boston for the purpose of thoroughly looking into the matter. The inspector has not reported yet, but I shall be very glad
to let the hon. gentleman see his report when it is received.
Then it is a fact that potatoes cannot be exported from Canada to the United States at the present time?
That is the position.
From what province in Canada were they shipped?
They were shipped from New Brunswick, and I have no doubt they were New Brunswick potatoes.

Since this difficulty
occurred, has the Department of Agriculture taken steps to supervise each shipment, in order that none of our potatoes so affected shall be exported?

I understand that the Department of Agriculture has inspectors at all the ports, watching shipments very closely. If there is anything wrong with the potatoes, the inspectors do not allow them , to go out of the country. Our inspectors think that the American authorities were not justified in condemning that shipment of potatoes to Boston. Every precaution is taken by the department to see that nothing is shipped unless in first-class condition.
Had this carload been inspected?
Yes.

After the minister received notice about this carload of potatoes shipped to Boston or New York- I understood that it was at New York that the difficulty occurred-did he take any steps to have the car examined by an intelligent inspector, or was nothing done in the matter? The reason I ask is that the potatoes in question were shipped, not only from my own constituency, but from my own home. On Saturday afternoon I had the privilege of interviewing an inspector of the Department of Agriculture, a very capable man indeed, who had received his training at Macdonald College, and he assured me in the most positive manner that the cars were personally inspected by him. He said that he had inspected practically every potato, and could not think it possible that there should be a diseased potato among them. I mention that because I think the Government should know it, and I would like to know if any further inspection was made in Boston or New York.

The hon. gentleman confirms what I said a few minutes ago, that in so far as the Department of Agriculture is con-

cerned the inspectors were taking every precaution to see that no potatoes left Canada except in proper condition. When Mr. O'Halloran. the Deputy Minister, brought this to my attention on Wednesday or Thursday of last week, I instructed him to send an inspector to Boston, to examine the potatoes thoroughly and make an official report. I do not see that I could have done other than that. At all events I gave instructions to do everything possible, to have them examined again thoroughly by an independent inspector and to make a report accordingly.

I would like to draw the attention of the hon. Minister of the Interior (Mr. Roche) to thajact that information has come to me to the effect that certain agents of the Government from Saskatchewan are refusing to accept applications for seed from men who are on patented lands and also that the Dominion lands agents at Wadena, Battleford and Big-gar are refusing to take any applications from men who have received their patents. I would like to ask the minister if, in view of the statement he made to this House on February 10 in which he agreed that every application should be given proper consideration, he has instructed the agents to receive and consider every application properly, whether the land of the applicant is patented or not.

The policy which was announced here by myself is being followed out, I believe, to the letter. Instructions were sent to the Commissioner, of Immigration, who has charge of this matter of the distribution of seed grain, to deal with cases coming from the holders of patented as well as unpatented lands in all deserving cases. Of course, there have been several thousand applications of cases that do not come under the enumeration that has been laid down, and they have therefore been refused. Mr. Bruce Walker was in the city on Saturday, and he told us that outside of the drought-stricken area 7,000 applications had been favourably acted upon.

speechtext:
I would like to say to the hon. member for Richmond (Mr. Kyte), who asked me to lay upon the table of the House some telegrams from Mr. H. C. Crowell of Halifax, that I expected to have them ready to lay upon the table of the House to-day; but I find that there are some [Mr. J. D. Reid.I
more to be filed and I will lay them on the table of the House to-morrow. I would like, however, to explain that it appears that the interview which was alluded to in the telegram from Sir George Perley was an interview with General Guy Carleton Jones, director of the Army Medical Service. The mistake occurred in this way, that the code word which was translated by the decoding clerk in this telegram as " Alderson " appears twice in the code book, and the decoding clerk selected the particular word which worked out as " Alderson." A further telegram from Sir George Perley explained that he had used the code word which appears elsewhere in the code book and which worked out as " Jones," and this was the word he intended to use. Therefore, Mr. Crowell is quite right in stating that he did not have an interview with General Aider-son, but nevertheless there was an interview with Surgeon General Jones, Director General of the Army Medical Service in England. It was he, as I am informed, who had the interview with Mr. Crowell in which Mr. Crowell expressed the opinion that has already been communicated to the House.

The House in Committee on Private Bills. Mr. Sevigny in the Chair.
Bill No. 8, respecting the Edmonton, Dun-vegan and British Columbia Railway Company-Mr. Green-in committee.
On section 1-extension of time for construction :

When this Bill was up on Friday night we had under discussion the time during which the company should have the right to start work, the provision being that it must be started within a period of two years. There was no disposition, as far as I understood the matter then under discussion, on the part of any person, to delay in any way the passing of the Bill, but in view of the fact that this railway company have already sold their bonds and have the money on hand, and as there is a pressing necessity for the construction of this line of railway, at all event from a point known as Smoky river to a point known as Spirit river, a distance of some fifty miles, it was thought that it might be well to make a reduction in the extension of time allowed for commencing the work from two years to a lesser period by reason of the fact that the conditions are favour-

able and also by reason of the fact that, as I understand it, those who are in charge of the work are not anxious for an extension of two years but are willing to carry on the work as soon as spring opens in so far as this fifty miles in particular is concerned. I think that perhaps the Chairman of the Railway Committee will be disposed to amend that clause and provide that work shall be commenced within a period of six months instead of two years. I think that would cover the difficulty, taken with the assurance we have from the railway people that they are going to go ahead with the work and that they propose to complete as speedily as possible the line from Smoky river to Spirit river.

Under the circumstances, I do not see any objection to the suggestion of the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat (Mr. Rogers). As I said on Friday night, we granted a time for commencing the unconstructed portions of these roads because some of the charters are already expiring. If we haa been sure in the railway committee that none of these franchises would run out before His Royal Highness would give his' consent to this Bill we would not have needed to have worried about the commencement. We would simply have said that they should be allowed five years to complete the uncompleted portions of their road. But the better opinion among lawyers is that when charters are expiring, or have expired, it is necessary to also give a time for commencing. Some of these franchises would expire in three or four days from now and it was necessary that we should resuscitate them. That is why the clause is worded as it is. The hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) remarked on Friday night about the peculiar language, and that is the explanation. If it were not so we would not have said anything about what is contained in the first five or six lines; we would simply have dealt with the time when they should complete the uncompleted portions of the road. In view of what was said on Friday night and, with the unanimous consent of the House, I will move to amend this clause by striking out the words " two years " and inserting in lieu thereof the words " six months " for commencement. T am assured by counsel representing the company that they propose going right on at once or as soon as this Bill is passed and the company do not object to this change. They will not object to being required to hurry on within six months. Therefore, in accordance with 46	'
the suggestion of my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works, I move to amend section I, by striking out the words " two years " in line three and inserting in lieu thereof the words " six months."

1 am sorry I was not in my seat on Friday evening when this Bill came up for discussion. I am not rising now particularly to object to the shortening of the time to six months. This Bill was discussed very fully in the Railway Committee, and it seems strange that it should for some reason or another have met with opposition, not only there but in the House. I wish to point out that this Bill is one that should receive every encouragement in this Parliament, because these people are railway builders; they are not people who are asking for anything unreasonable; they are in the business of building that particular railway, as evidenced by the fact that they have already built and have laid the steel upon 262 miles of that railway. Their charter expires oh the 17th day of March, a few days hence, and it is necessary, as the Chairman of the Railway Committee pointed out, to have the extension granted at this particular time, so as to prevent its expiration, and inability to reinstate it if it is not signed by the Governor General before the date of expiration. These people have not only built the road so far, but they have the money on hand to continue construction. The line of railway is northerly from Edmonton to mile 131 where the railway crosses the Athabasca river. The bridge over this river is of steel on concrete piers. The route from the crossing of the river is generally westerly along the south shore of the Lesser Slave lake, and through the settled district just west of Lesser Slave lake. From the end of steel, grading has been done to a point a short distance east of Smoky river, and it is proposed when the frost goes out of the ground to continue the grading and lay the steel in a westerly direction. The intention is to construct the line of Tailway to Peace River block, where it will join with the Pacific Great Eastern railway, a line of railway which is being built through the province of British Columbia. Bonds for 350 miles of the railway, to the extent of 820,000 per mile, were guaranteed by the province of Alberta, the Tate of interest being 41 peT cent. It is the intention of the company to push work vigorously for the obvious reason that the company is anxious to obtain all available



freight from Spirit River and from Grande Prairie. The company is seeking legislation at the present session to enable it to forthwith construct a line of railway from a point on its main line near Spirit River settlement through Grande Prairie, with the object of giving relief at as early a date as possible to the settlement in Grande Prairie.
When this charter was before the Railway Committee, objection was taken by some members of the committee that the government of Alberta, being interested as guarantors of the bonds, should be consulted. They were consulted by telegram by the Hon. the Minister of Railways, and he had a reply from the Premier of that province saying that they had no fault to find with the Bill as it was, and that under the contract for the guarantee, they were in a good position to protect the province from any attempt on the part of these people to forego construction at the present time. There is no desire at all on the part of the contractors to retard construction, because the line already built is of no service until it is extended to meet the requirements and to get the trade of certain districts which are settled. The country through which the line is already built is not settled to any great extent, and therefore these people are particularly desirous of continuing the work, so as to reach the settled districts. I repeat that I have no desire to oppose the amendment offered by the Chairman of the Railway Committee, that the period be reduced from two years to six months. I think, however, it would have been better to give a year, but six months is quite satisfactory to the promoters of the railway, and I think by the time this House meets again we will find that the railway has not only been completed to the confines of the province of Alberta, but that it has probably been connected up with the Pacific Great Eastern railway of British Columbia.

My hon. friend (Mr. Green) says he cannot understand why there is opposition to this Bill, both in the committee and in the House. I desire, as a member, to protest against any hon. gentleman saying it means opposition to a Bill, simply because a member wants to have it put in proper form. The Bill in its present form is decidedly objectionable. It is all very well to say that the gentlemen who are building this road are railway builders. I know they are. I know that Mr. Macdonald, who is the principal party concerned in the

building of the road, is a gentleman of the very highest character and may be expected to push the road forward as Tapidly as possible. But, every time we pass a Bill in this House we are forming a precedent for future legislation, and under this legislation as it is, the company need not strike another blow, even on the portion of the road on wfhich the steel has been laid, but which may not be completed because it is not ballasted or because station-houses have not been built. I cannot for the life of me see why it is necessary to put any provision in the Bill as to the commencement of construction upon the uncompleted portion. The road lias been commenced under the provisions of the charter, and all that would be necessary would be to provide a time for completion, but under this Bill the company can lie down to-morrow and not strike another blow for two years, and not complete that portion of the road which may be practically constructed. That is why I took objection to the form of the Bill. I had no idea of opposing the measure, nor had I any idea of throwing any obstruction in the way of the company. I am quite sure that the Minister of Public Works, in the views he expressed in the committee, had no such thought either. But what I wanted was to endeavour to have proper legislation passed so that in regard to the road which is under way the company should be compelled to go right ahead with as reasonable speed as possible.

I fail to see how an
amendment to this Bill, making it incumbent on the railway company to commence construction within six months, is going to assist in the speedy construction of the road. I would point out that the policy of the Railway Committee of this House, in recent years, has been to have some uniform time fixed, to which charters should be extended. I think the chairman of the committee will bear me out in saying that until last year the policy of the Railway Committee for the two previous years had been that where a railway company had not commenced the construction of a road to give it two years to commence and five years to finish, if it was an ordinary railway. Last year an innovation was made in the Railway Committee, and instead of granting two years, the policy of granting one year was adopted.

My hon. friend can
hardly call that a policy. What we concluded was that each tub should stand on its own bottom, and that each Bill should be

dealt with on its own unique facts and particular merits, believing that there might be cases in which in the interest of the public and not too harmful to the progress of the company, they should be cut down to one year. We did that in some cases and refused to do it in others. So far as I was concerned, I advised in the committee-perhaps advised is too strong a word to use-but I suggested that each Bill should be treated on its own special merits. And where one company might get two years to commence and five years to finish, another company might get only one year to commence, and, in fact, in some cases, it might not be found desirable to extend the charter at all. It was not a policy for any fixed time exactly that was laid down by the com. mittee.

Until last year the policy of the Railway Committee was to give companies which, had not commenced , com struction two years to commence and five years finish. Last year some of the members of the committee thought that was too long, and in some instances the time for commencement was cut down to one year. When the extension of time for this railway was challenged in the Railway Committee, I took the ground that if we were going to cut down the time in which to commence to construct the uncompleted portion of the road, we should also reduce the time for completion; that is, if we gave the company six months in which to commence construction, we should give it three years instead of five years in which to finish, because it is not going to help out the completion of the road to limit the time in which the company may commence operations and to let it have five years in which to complete. I am sure that every hon. member, whatever part of Canada he may come from, is anxious to see this road built; and if this amendment calling for commencement of construction within six months is to go through, another amendment should be made that the road should be finished within three years.

My opinion is that it does not necessarily. follow, that because you cut down the time for commencement of construction to six months, you should also cut down the time for completion from five years to three. When a company has commenced construction and has spent and is spending money on its road, for its own sake it will endeavour to complete the road as soon as possible, because it gets no 46i
revenue until the jpad is completed. Obstru-tions may arise preventing the completion of the road within the three years; and there is no harm in giving the company five years, so long as it is going ahead with the construction.
Why not give the company two years in which to commence construction?
That is a different matter entirely.

The hon. Minister of
Public Works is anxious for the completion of the railway, and he is right in taking the stand that he does. He will not, however, accomplish his purpose by giving the company a short limit in which to commence operations and five years in which to complete the road.
He will accomplish it by forcing the company into an undertaking on which it will lose interest and from which it cannot possibly get any profit or revenue until the road is completed.

Very unfair discrimination is being shown against this Tailway company. Ever since I have been a member of this House, in the Railway Committee we have been extending charters for railway companies. A premium is being put on railway companies which do not do anything. This railway company has done more actual construction in -a given space of time than any other company in Alberta. It has completed 262 miles of its line and has a service on that portion; it has in addition 25 miles of steel laid. This railway runs through a country which is not productive of freight or revenue up to the point which it has reached at the present time, namely 262 miles from Edmonton; but from now on the company is bound to make revenue by pushing its line forward. There is no question of commencement at all, because the railway company has never ceased constructing its line. It is doing construction work at the present time. It is merely on account of the fluctuations of the market that it is asking for an extension of time. I do not think that the committee is dealing fairly with this particular railway company in limiting it to six months for commencement of construction.
The company is not raising any objection.

That is not the point. This section is not going to hinder the com-

pany in the least, because it is going right on at present with the construction of its line. The point is that there is unfair discrimination against this particular railway company. That is why I object to this section. It will not affect -the Edmonton, Dunvegan and British Columbia Railway Company, if you put the time to commence construction at ten days. This is the point: Is this committee going to single out this particular line of railway and insist on a six months' limit for commencement, when companies owning charters f-or railways going through this same section of country - are doing nothing whatever to earn their charters?
As regards the settlement in the country through which this railway runs, I saw a clipping the other day which stated that in 1914 there were 1,280 homestead entries in the Peace River agencies and 913 in the Grande Prairie agencies. This railway does not project far into the Grande Prairie district; but when it reaches Spirit river it will come within fifty miles of -the Grand Prairie country, and I am informed by men who know that during the coming summer this railway will reach the Spirit river, giving communication to the people of the Grande Prairie district within fifty miles of this railway. I do not contend that it will hamper the company in any way to insert the six months' limit.

I can assure my hon.
friend that there is no intention on the part of any hon. member to place any lunfair restriction on this particular railway or to treat it in any way that could be termed unfair. On the contrary, as I understand the disposition of hon. members on both sides, they are well disposed to give this railway company every assistance and every consideration possible. I was moved to make the remarks I did by reason of the fact that a couple of years ago we had a deputation from the Grande Prairie district, which is forty or fifty miles from Spirit river. This railway company had its charter ; it had its bonds sold and had the money ready with which to go on and build the line from Smoky river to Spirit river. What the people from the Grande Prairie district had in view was the clause in this extension, namely, that the company was to have two years in which to build the line from Smoky river as far as Spirit river, a line which interests particularly the people -of the Grande Prairie district. They were hoping to get a local line with which to connect

with this railway, to enable them to ship their grain. On the deputation there was one farmer who had in his granary over
65,000	bushels of grain. Hon. members can understand the temper and feeling of people who grow grain in such large quantities as that: they pay very careful attention to the wording of any extension of time granted to any railway that is likely to give them relief. There is no objection on the part of this railway company to the time limit being fixed at six months. If the company were not satisfied with that time limit, and if there were any difficulty from any point of view, I would not press the point; but in view of the anxiety of the people of the Grand Prairie district for railway communication, I thought it only fair for us to give them such consideration as we could. So far as I am aware, there is no intention on the part of any hon. member to place any difficulty in the way of this company going on with its work. As all parties are agreed as to this change of time, I do not see why there should be any objection to it.

I am not voicing any
objection; I am merely stating that it will not hamper the railway company to have this amendment inserted. If the minister is sincere in his desire to assist the people in Grande Prairie, he will take the same stand as he is taking at present, when the Bill respecting the Canadian Northern railway comes up.

Will this railway serve
the people of Grande Prairie or will it not?
It will come within fifty miles.
That is a good distance to walk.

As regards these extensions of time for railways, last session I favoured a limited extensio'n and I favour it to-day. I am also in favour of the view taken by the hon. member for South Cape Breton (Mr. Carroll), that the time for completion should be reduced if the time for commencement is reduced. Western Canada is plastered with railroad charters. Extensions are granted year after year, but construction is not proceeded with. Present financial conditions may be an excuse for delay in completing railroad lines, but generally speaking I think it would be better for western Canada if many of these railway charters were cancelled. Settlers

have been living in isolated districts in anticipation of the construction of railroads and their hopes are not being realized on account of these everlasting extensions. This applies to districts in all parts of Western Canada. The need is not so great in sections of the country which already possess railway transportation facilities, but I think that a railway company proposing to build into a section of the country where there are no railroads should not be given continued extensions of time; it is a discouragement to the people. If this general principle were adopted, the people of districts in western Canada which are not provided with railroads would be in a position to know whether or not they are to have railway communication.

The hon. gentleman evidently did not hear the explanation I made a few moments ago. This is not a paper charter. The company have no objection to the reduction of time to six months, but it would be manifestly unfair not to treat them as Other companies are treated so far as the time of completion is concerned. These people are on the ground, spending money every day on the construction of this railway. They have so much of it built that they must of necessity continue construction, or they will get no business.
I am quite in favour of limiting the time in respect of companies with paper charters, but in view of the fact that these people have the money and are prepared to continue construction, I think it would be too , had if we should not meet them on all possible points.

I cannot for the life of me see what good or harm this motion can do anybody. If the company were ready and willing to go on, the changing of the time limit would not hurry them a bit; if they were hanging back and did not want to go on, I would see some reason for the proposed amendment. It all depends upon what we mean by commencement.
I have known holders of charters to work a team and scraper four hours, and call that a commencement of a railway line. Such provisions look well in the statute, but my experience is that anything we have so far done to compel companies to commence construction has not amounted to much. Almost anything may constitute a commencement; the important consideration is the time within which the line must be completed. If this motion is passed other companies will be asked to accept a similar
condition. In some future application for extension of time, a reference to the statute will show that in this instance Parliament imposed a six-months' limit, and that, therefore, the same limit should be imposed in the case under consideration. This would, perhaps, make the proposed operations prohibitive.
I think the Railway Committee should deal with each separate charter on its own merits.

That is a good theory, but in many respects we are creatures of precedent; the special pleader
4 p.m. always quotes precedent. If by this proposed amendment anything were to he accomplished in the interests of the people who want this railway, there would be no reason why it should not be adopted, but, so far as I can see, it will accomplish nothing. If Parliament is afraid that the company will not proceed with the work, the six-months' limit will not make any difference; the company can go on just the same under the Bill as it now stands.

I know the company will be perfectly satisfied with this amendment; otherwise I would agree with the hon. gentleman.

Bill No. 17, respecting the Canadian Pacific railway-Mr. W. H. Sharpe-in committee.
On section 2-extension of time for completion :

To what particular
branches of road does paragraph D of section 2 of chapter 96 of the Statutes of 1913 refer?

That is from a point on the Kleinburg-Sudbury branch, between Bolton junction and Palgrave, and westerly through the counties of Peel and Halton to a point on the Ontario and Quebec railway near Canipbellville.
On section 4:
The company may sell, lease or charter any steam or other vessels of the company to the Canadian Pacific Ocean Services Limited, an incorporated company, or to any other incorporated company duly empowered to acquire, hold, own, maintain or operate steam or other vessels upon such terms and for such considerations as may be determined by the boards of directors of the companies respectively.

This clause and the succeeding clause in the Bill, which gives power to hold shares of the Ocean Services Company, make the most radical change that has yet been made in the policy of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. If I read this Bill aright, and if I understand the explanations that were offered at the Railway Committee, the proposal of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company is to sell to the Canadian Pacific Ocean Services, Ltd., a company that is to be organized, any of its steam or ocean vessels, upon such terms as may be determined on by the board of directors of the companies respectively. The Canadian Pacific railway has been a'great national proposition in this country. It has been largely subsidized by the country in land, finished railway, money and many other concessions that were given to it. Eventually it was completed from ocean to ocean. It has been raised to the position of being the greatest railroad under any one corporation in the world. It has had a most successful career. The progress of Canada has been identified with that of the Canadian Pacific railway; and it may be said that the credit of Canada has been upheld, in a sense, by this railroad. Recently an announcement was made that there was to be a change in the policy of the railway, it was said that it was the intention of the company hereafter to segregate the extraneous assets of the company. That was announced by the president of the company at public meetings and at the meetings of the shareholders. I understand that the proposal of the company now is to dismember this great national railway in which Canada has such a vital interest, and that the first 
thing to be dismembered will be the ocean steamships. It was proposed, when this Bill first came to the Railway Committee that they were also to take away the lake steamships, but they found that they could not do that, and so withdrew that proposal. They propose now, in this very simple clause, to begin the dismemberment of the great Canadian Pacific railway, to take the ocean steamships out of its jurisdiction and put them under another company called the Canadian Pacific Ocean Services, Ltd. We got the information in the committee the other day that this Canadian Pacific Railway Ocean Services, Ltd., is a company that is to be incorporated under the Joint Stock Companies Act of Great Britain; and, once it is incorporated there, it is without the jurisdiction of the Canadian Parliament, and so the ocean steamship service is beyond any interference by the people or the Parliament of Canada. This new company, we were informed, is to have an immense capitalization. We have the old company and its great capitalization, and we are now having established in England another company with large capitalization and large bonding powers under British . control, absolutely out of the control of Canada. You will notice that this Ocean Services Company is to acquire the steamboats on such terms and for such consideration as may be determined by the board of directors of the companies respectively. That is, the Canadian Pacific Railway is to appoint the directors of the two companies, and so can, on any terms it likes, transfer the ocean steamships to the new company, and thus remove them from the jurisdiction of Canada.
Was it the intention of the original charter that this great road should be dismembered and the assets passed over to another company over which we have no jurisdiction?
I never heard of suchr a proposal as that, of Parliament giving up its jurisdiction over a matter of such great national interest as the Canadian Pacific railway.
Have we control over the ocean rates now?

I say that we can get
control.
Have we control now?

I think we have. I will ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce whether he was not a member of the Royal Commission appointed in Great Britain to consider our jurisdiction in this matter. Until we find out just what our jurisdiction is, I do not propose to abandon the powers

we now have. I would find a way of controlling the ocean rates of the Canadian Pacific Railway, and I am certainly not going to make confession in this House that we have no jurisdiction over that matter.
The hon. gentleman stated that we had control, and were giving up control.

I am not going to argue that to-day. Non possumus is a very good argument, but I am not going to adduce it in this case. I do not think any one who knows that great road and the great work it has done could make such a confession at this time. What is happening is this: We are giving power to a British company over which we have no control. That is perfectly certain. Once this British company is created we have no control over it, and I contend that we can have control over ocean rates. The fifth clause provides that the Canadian Pacific Railway may guarantee the securities of the Canadian Pacific Ocean Services Limited. That is, we are not only putting the steamships outside the jurisdiction of this House by turning them over to a British company, but we are giving to the Canadian Pacific Railway power to guarantee the securities of a company outside of our jurisdiction. That is the effect of this Act. It is a very simple proposal, and yet to my mind the most radical proposal that was ever put forward in connection with the Canadian Pacific Railway. And the company brings it forward just after the Government have brought down an amendment to the Railway Act containing a clause for the regulation of the financial operations of any railway company in this country. One of the clauses of the Bill introduced by the Minister of Railways last session says in substance, that no company shall issue any stock, shares, certificates of stock, bonds, debentures, debenture stock, notes, mortgage or other securities without first obtaining leave of the board. Then there is this clause:
The board as it deems the circumstances warrant, may refuse or may grant leave for the proposed issue or may grant leave for such part thereof as it is satisfied is reasonable and proper, and may in any case impose any terms or conditions it may deem proper.
Last session the Government committed themselves, and brought in a very good Bill to amend the Railway Act. The Bill contained the two clauses I have just read,
namely, that the issue of securities by any railroad of this country must first be approved by the Railway Commission, who can impose terms in any respect they like.
Is that the law now?

By reason of the lateness of the session last year the Government postponed its Railway Bill for another session. They have not brought down the Bill this year; so I have brought down a Public Bill in my own name, and it is now before the Railway Committee. So this radical proposal in connection with the Canadian Pacific railway is made just -after the Government announced its intention of amending the Railway Act. My contention is that if the Government intend to make that Bill the law of the land- and I believe they do-this Bill of the Canadian Pacific Railway ought to be delayed until the Railway Act is amended. If the Government measure can wait for one session, so can the proposal of the Canadian Pacific Railway; or if one goes through, both should go through; and the amendment I shall bring up to-day will be in that direction.
I pointed out in the Railway Committee the other day that the Canadian Pacific railway was a great national undertaking, and that its original charter contained a clause which ought to be of great interest to the House to-day. What I am speaking of is partly set out in the preamble and partly in a subsequent clause. The preamble"' says:
Whereas by the terms and conditions of the admission of British Columbia into union with the Dominion of Canada, the Government of the Dominion has assumed the obligation of causing a railway to be constructed, connecting the seaboard of British Columbia with the railway system of Canada ;.. . and it is necessary for the development of the Northwest Territory and for the preservation of the good faith of the Government in the performance of its obligations, that immediate steps should be taken to complete and operate the whole of the said railway;
And the last sentence in section 7 says:
And the company shall thereafter and for ever efficiently maintain, work and run the Canadian Pacific railway.
We not only gave these bonuses and gifts to the Canadian Pacific railway, we not only built that road because it was an essential part of Confederation and because we had to do it in fulfilment of our obligation, but we imposed on the Canadian Pacific railway-and it is imposed on no other railway in this country-that the

undertaking should be maintained as a railway for ever, and as a first class Tailway at that. And now, before we have revised our Railway Act, we propose to allow this company to begin its work of dismembering its assets. Por this 'proposal, as shown by a statement of Sir Thomas Shaughruessy's the other day, is only one of -a 'Series of movements to dismember this railway. They first propose to dismember the steamship service.
I have not read the original charter. Does it provide that the Company must establish a line of ocean steamships ?

I do not say that it does. But a great national unde taking has grown up by reason of the aid given to that company by this Parliament^; and now that company proposes to enter upon a policy of dismemberment.
Not to dismember the railway

This means the dismemberment of the railway, as I shall show. Sir Thomas Shaughnessy pointed out the other day that it was the intention of the company to segregate their extraneous assets. In plain English, that is they are going to dismember the road; they are going to cut the limbs off the trunk, and I call that the dismemberment of the Canadian Pacific railway.
Can the Canadian Pacific Railway sell their steamers to another company ?

Perhaps they can, but
I am not going to give them power to put the security of the Canadian Pacific Railway behind this other company.
Where is the vice in what the hon. gentleman has just said"'

I am coming to the
vice. I can* hardly get a chance to make my case here. You would think I had a most vicious intention judging from the attitude of some hon. gentlemen towards my proposals, whereas I am merely trying to protect the public interest in regard to this Canadian Pacific railway which we have subsidized so generously in the past. Sir Thomas Shaughnessy says that he proposes to segregate the extraneous assets. He is going to lop off the steamship company. Hon. gentlemen say he can do that already. I do not know whether he can or not, but I am not going to help him to

do so by legislation in this House. He said:	I am going to dismember the lake
steamship service which is absolutely a part of the service within Canada. He found he could not do that so he withdrew from that position. He has further stated that they are going to dismember the lands and townsites and put them under another company. If they get that power they will then dismember the express, hotel and telegraph system and in the end we will only be a trunk line of railway with a capitalization of $235,000,000 or more and the other securities that have been issued on the Canadian Pacific Railway. All other assets will be put into other companies with different capitalizations. The result will be that the Canadian Pacific Railway and its associates and all the work that it is now doing under the original charter, and it is doing all this work under the original charter, will have a capitalization of two or three times what the capitalization is at present and the people who pay the freight will have to pay heavier charges as a consequence. It is not in the public interest that we should allow the company to dismember its various assets. Counsel for the railway when they appeared before the Railway Committee stated that they intended to keep control of these assets, that the stock of the new company which they would receive for the steamships which they sold would be placed in the treasury of the Canadian Pacific Railway. When they were asked if they had any objection to a clause being put in this Bill defining that, and saying that the Canadian Pacific Railway shall hold all this stock for the benefit of the public, they refused to consent to it. They may have some other intention in regard to the stock. It may be that they propose to distribute this stock in the new company among their shareholders or it may be that there will be a new melon cut for the benefit of those in whose interest this legislation is being asked. It is not in the public interest that this great railway should be dismembered or that the proceeds of the dismemberment should be used by the company for the benefit of the shareholders. There is no guarantee that such a distribution among the shareholders will not take place. Do we want to have control of ocean services in Canada? Do the people of Canada suffer now from the fact that heretofore we have not been able to control ocean services in Canada whether they were connected with our railways or not? Is it not the case that a commission appointed by one of the provinces of the West found that the high freight

rates in connection with the movement of the grain of the West was due to the high ocean freight rates? That was found to be absolutely the case. The millers of the country are on record as protesting against excessive ocean freight rates. The people of Ontario and the hoards of trade of Ontario and of Montreal have protested against excessive ocean freight rates. To-day the fact exists that, notwithstanding all we are doing for the farmers of the West, notwithstanding the distribution of seed grain and of feed, the farmers of the Canadian West, at the prices which they have obtained in recent years for their wheat, will not be able to stay on their land and make a living if they get the same kind of treatment in regard to ocean freight rates that they have got in the past five years. Notwithstanding the fact that the farmers of the West are faced by the conditions brought about by the war, notwithstanding that the railways have recently got an increase in the freight rates in the West, or some modifications-perhaps it may have been a reduction-the railway companies are now down before the railway commission asking for an increase in rates. When the West is stricken by one thing and another, and especially by reason of the recent bad year-not b.y the war-
A restricted market.

I am not for a restricted market. When we are faced with these conditions, two things happen: The Canadian Pacific Railway is getting absolutely clear from its steamships <so that the Parliament of Canada cannot control it in that respect, and it is getting ready to put up the freight rates and to dismember all the other portions of the system over [DOT]which Parliament has had control. Is that a thing to do to-day ? We are likely to have further trouble in the Canadian West if we allow the Canadian Pacific Railway to take these steamship lines away and put them under a British company, thus leaving them free to raise the rates. At the same time we aTe going to allow them to evade this new law, which the Government proposed last session and which 1 have introduced this session, giving the Board of Railway Commissioners control over the capitalization of railway companies. It is not good policy to do that. It is not in line with the policy of Sir John A. Macdonald, who built this Canadian Pacific railway. He built that road for ever, and the bigger it got the better pleased he was with it. The greater it
became from his time to that of the Administrations subsequent to him the more it became the pride of this country. But now like a flash, and in two innocent little paragraphs, the Canadian Pacific Railway is here asking forv power to dismember itself.
No.
Yes, they are asking for power to take away these steamship lines. They came with a proposal to dismember the lake steamships. Here is what Sir Thomas Shaughnessy says-
That was all amended in the Railway Committee.

Yes, it was all very nicely fixed up. Sir Thomas Shaughnessy said:
It is only another step in the direction ot eliminating from the direct operation of the railway company items that do not relate to the railway property itself.
The railway property itself, according to Sir Thomas Shaughnessy, means the road bed and the stations, but all the other things are not considered a part of the railway. He would dismember this great corporation that we have built up, take away all these auxiliary services and leave only the railway service. That was not the original intention. That is not how this road has grown to the enormous proportions which it has attained to-day. Now we have before us a proposition for its dismemberment, its breaking up, and we have information to that effect in this statement by Sir Thomas Shaughnessy given to the public the otheT day.
What' is the real object of this Bill ? In view of the fact that we are likely in this Parliament to get jurisdiction over the steamship lines, they are going, with our assistance if they can, to place the steamship lines in a British company over which we shall have no jurisdiction. They are going to establish this British company fox the creation of a great steamship service. This British company, with its large capital, will have ships on the Atlantic and ships on the Pacific, and own the vessels that the Canadian Pacific Railway own today, but not under the jurisdiction of this Parliament.
Are not all the Canadian Pacific Railway steamships at present registered in England?

There is another of
these questions that they bring up.
I merely wanted to know for information.

I do not know whether they are or not, but we will admit that they are. Now I am coming to the point, and that is where we will be tested by the people of the country. We do propose to allow this dismemberment to begin, and it is proposed to allow it to apply to the ocean steamships, and it is proposed to *create a British company outside our jurisdiction. That may be possible, and at all events it is being done now, and no matter what any hon. member may say, or no matter what excuse he may offer for the Canadian Pacific Railway, I want to ask him whether he is prepared to do this? After we have created this great company and taken over these steamships, here is the next clause of the Bill:
The company (that is, the Canadian Pacific Railway) may guarantee the securities of the Canadian Pacific Railway Ocean Services, Limited.
Now, the Canadian Pacific Railway Ocean Services, Limited, is, as everbody will see, for the express purpose of creating a great sea monopoly beyond control of Canada, beginning with the boats of the Canadian Pacific Railway on the Atlantic and Pacific oceans, and every ocean they may go upon. And when they have done that and when they have lopped this limb off and given it to the other Company, they propose that this Parliament of Canada shall authorize the Canadian Pacific Railway to endorse the securities, no matter to what extent, that may be issued by this foreign company, in order to create and build up and strengthen the greatest sea monopoly that ever was in the world. There will be no monopoly on the seas equal to this new monopoly the Canadian Pacific Railway propose to build up. They propose to put boats on every sea, they propose to put them under the jurisdiction of a British Act, where we have no control whatever, and they propose to do it all on the credit of the Canadian Pacific Railway, and the Canadian Parliament is asked to endorse that proposal and to give this power. Goodness knows it is bad enough to stand all we have stood in the past, and it is bad enough for the farmers of the Canadian West to have suffered from excessive ocean rates in the past. And we are distributing free seed grain among the farmers of the West, and when

these great railways are coming to ask for higher rates, is that a time to go a step further and give to the Canadian Pacific railway power to guarantee the securities of this company, for building up a great monopoly to unfairly treat the people of Canada? There is the issue, and that is the issue that will come home to the people of this country, and that is the issue I present to the Government and especially to the Minister of Railways. I say that is not good policy. I say it is not good policy at this time to give this great power of segregation. I say it is absolutely mis-policy; I say it is against the public interest; I say it is against the interests of the farmers of the West that the Canadian Pacific Railway should be allowed to cut a rod to beat the backs of our own Canadian people. That is the issue, and you cannot get away from it, and that issue is now up to this Parliament. What business have we to allow the Canadian Pacific Railway to build up a corporation outside of our own country, and on the strength of its own credit, in order to use unfairly the people of Canada? There have been excessive ocean charges in the past, and the Canadian Pacific Railway feel they are in a way responsible, because they are in the great ocean combine, and they fear we might find a way to get at them through the commission of which the Minister of Trade and Commerce is a member, and to put them under our jurisdiction. I know there is a way yet to be found to get them under our jurisdiction with regard to these ocean freight rates, and now they are trying to get away from that. Are we going to let them get away from us under this clause which empowers them to endorse the notes of this foreign company and. this hostile company to the Canadian people? And it is to be a hostile company to Canada so far as ocean rates are concerned. They are trying now to get away from our jurisdiction; they fear we have jurisdiction, or that the Empire will find a way to get jurisdiction over them, and at such a time we are letting them go and giving them these privileges which they can exercise as they like. If the Bill to amend the Railway Act, introduced by the Government last session, was good law, and if the same Bill which I have introduced this session is good law-
Suppose the amendment to the Railway Act had been passed last year, how would it affect this matter?

It would affect it to the extent that the Canadian Pacific Railway would not be allowed to guarantee these

bonds without the consent of the Railway Commission.
I think the hon. gentleman is wrong there.
Why should that Act not provide for that?

Does the hon. gentleman think he is referring to the Act correctly?
Mr.-MACLEAN: I think so. Anyhow, if such a provision is not there it ought to be there, and what the Minister of Railways undertook to do was to put the securities of these railway companies under the control of the Railway Commission. That is what they are doing in the States, that is what we ought to do here, but we are very slow in doing it, and while we are slow in doing it the Canadian Pacific Railway is trying to get away from us. Is it calculated to advance the settlement of the Canadian West that we should let these steamships get away from us and let them get under a foreign company?
Does the hon. gentleman call a British company a "foreign" company?
As regards this legislation, yes. I am surprised at the loyalty of the hon. gentleman from the Baie des Chaleurs.
The hon. gentleman is old enough to remember the discussion which once took place in this House on the word " foreign."

I did not take part in
that discussion. At all events, the least that can be said of this is, that it is an extraneous company; it is a company over which we have no control, and it is to be incorporated so that we cannot have control over it. But we have control over the Canadian Pacific railway, and we have control *over the securities of the Canadian Pacific railway, and that is a point which is easily grasped by the ordinary people of this country, and we are allowing the Canadian Pacific railway to endorse the securities of a company that is to build up a great ocean combine over which the people complain we will have no control.
How could one company build up a combine within itself?

In the very way that the Canadian Pacific railway has built it up now. The Canadian Pacific railway is a member of the North Atlantic steamship
combine, and if I were the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Railways, before I would pass this legislation I would say to the Canadian Pacific railway:	I will allow you to do some of
these things if you first give us a pledge that you will come out of the North Atlantic steamship combine. The dominant force up to date in the North Atlantic steamship combine is the Canadian Pacific railway, and the people most ill-used under it are the people of Canada.
How can it be the greatest; what about the Cunard line and the White Star line?

They are not greater
than the Canadian Pacific railway, but even if they are, they are out of our jurisdiction, and if the little villain is under our jurisdiction let us get hold of him. Let us not let him escape because there is a bigger villain elsewhere. You can argue from now until doomsday, but the point is that at a time when our western farmers and our Canadian merchants generally are complaining of excessive railway freight rates, and excessive ocean rates, and at a time when the doctrine is being set up that we have no jurisdiction over ocean rates, we are allowing the Canadian Pacific railway to put its ships into another company, and we are giving it the power to guarantee the securities of this foreign company to an unlimited amount, to create a still greater ocean combine and to terrorize uie people of Canada to a still greater extent in the future. That is not good Canadiain policy; that is not the National Policy; that was not the intention of Sir John A. Macdonald. It is not an up-to-date policy in connection with this great railway proposition. In the States to-day they have ordered some of the companies that built up extraneous assets to dismember. For instance, a lot of the coal companies which became railway companies, and railway companies which became coal companies more than they were railway companies, have been ordered by various authorities to disband, and to reorganize, and they have reorganized into other companies.
An hon. member near me says that is what is proposed to be done by this Bill. If the Canadian Pacific Railway do this, let us have control of the way in which they do it. Let us not give them a free hand to do as they like. When they are doing it, let us not give them a free hand to use the credit of the Canadian Pacific Railway

Company to build up the greatest ocean combine in the world. My contention is that they should snot be allowed to use their capitalization for that purpose. We did not build up the Canadian Pacific Railway Company and give them land and money and railway lines for the purpose of letting them use their capitalization for the establishment of an outside ocean steamship service that we cannot control, that will put up the freight rates and that will put our farmers out of business. If we allow the Canadian Pacific Railway Company to form an independent steamship company, we shall have to go a step further and find a remedy. That remedy will be the creation of a great ocean service, and we cannot entrust it to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. If this dismemberment which is under way goes on, we shall have to create a great merger with which to fight the Canadian Pacific Railway Company in this policy. We may have to merge two or three railways that at the present time have a hard struggle for existence, and to link them up with the Canadian Pacific railway and the Transcontinental. If we do that, we shall have to buy ocean steamships, and we may have to pay a very much larger sum now for the chartering of ocean steamships than we would have had to pay some time ago. If this dismemberment goes on, we shall have to nationalize the railways and our steamships on the oceans, or we may as well let our farmers in the Canadian West go out of business. It is a crazy-quilt policy to subsidize and to encourage farming in the West, and then in the East to allow a great company to create on the ocean a steamship monopoly with which to take all the products of the farmer away from him, following the policy of some American companies in the early days, which said: How much can we take from the farmer and still keep him as a poor man on the land? In western Canada we have pretty nearly reached that stage at the present time; and we would have done so if it had not been for the increased prices that the farmers are getting this year because of the war. If Siberia should go more into wheat production; and if that great country Persia, that may be opened up by reason of this war, and the countries in the valley of the Tigris and the Euphrates, which is a better wheat-growing section than is western Canada-do the same, our farmers under our excessive freight rates will be put out of business. 
These freight rates are charged by a company which we are allowing to pass out of our jurisdiction and on the flotations of stock on which we are placing no limitations. The Canadian Pacific Railway can give this steamship company any amount of credit, and there is not a line in this legislation to provide that, if the company wants to do certain things, it must go to some authority and get its approval. By this Bill, the company can do as it likes; it can issue stock to its shareholders at a low rate, as was done recently. .There has been no control of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company in the past, and it does not propose that we shall have any control of it in the future. Is the Parliament of Canada about to give the power to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company to do this thing that is improper and contrary to the interest of the public? The Canadian Pacific Railway Company are asking for this power, and I gather that the Government proposes to give it to them. I do not, however, propose that they shall have that power without my protest and the protest of the portion of the country from which I come. The people of Ontario are against the capitalization of railway companies being beyond Government control. Last year the Government took over the control of the finances of the Canadian Northern Railway Company. That is a beginning, and a good one.
Was that what the Government did last year?

We have control of the capitalization. We may not have control of the securities, but some of them at least are guaranteed by the Government., We took control of the capital stock. The amount of that is stated in the Act and the .company cannot increase it. That company was compelled to put all its operations into one system, and we have it more or less under control. We ought to have the Canadian Pacific Railway Company under control. This legislation is not in the public interest, and it is not legislation that we should put through during this time of war.
It has been stated that it is the policy of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company to dismember certain of its operations, such as telegraphs, hotels and lands. The Canadian Pacific Railway Company to-day owns lands that it got from the Government or that it purchased by means of money that came from the Government, that are worth from $200,000,000 to $500,000,000. It is proposed

next to take out those lands and put them into a like independent company, and use that as a melon for distribution among its shareholders. These lands and moneys *vrhich were given to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company were ear-marked for the benefit of the undertaking and not for the benefit of the shareholders. The contention is made that the shareholders can do, as they like with these things. They can do what they like only in the light and interpretation of the Act of Incorporation which was for the creation of a great transcontinental railway for the purpose of binding the provinces together. The railway company has used those lands and moneys to build itself up to the strength to which it has attained, and it should therefore not be allowed to dismember^ It is not good policy to allow it to take this land out of the company. I want to see the Canadian Pacific Railway Company keep itself intact. If it has in its treasury enormous reserves, which it is now trying to get rid of, those reserves are dedicated, consecrated and ear-marked according to my interpretation of the original charter, for the mitigation of railway freight charges and not for excessive dividends to the shareholders. Are we to sit quietly by and to allow this dismemberment to go on until there is nothing left but the trunk with the severed limbs?
If the Canadian Pacific Railway Company sells these steamships now to the new company, there is no intention that the proceeds realized from the sale shall be used for the reduction of the existing capitalization. The dismemberment is to go on, but the old capitalization is to remain, and the new proposition is all on new capital. The Canadian Pacific Railway Company in a very short time-and it says it is to keep in touch with all these new companies and to have control of them in some way-will have a capitalization of $500,000,000 instead of $250,000,000, as it is now. We are therefore authorizing a great exploitation and increase of the securities of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company in one way or another, and we are not keeping control of it. We have some control over the Canadian Pacific Railway Company in regard to certain stock issues, because the company has to come to the Governor in Council and get authority to issue it. I believe the Government of the hon. gentlemen opposite gave the company that authority on two or three occasions.
Under this most dangerous legislation the credit of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company will be used to build up a great ocean combine, over which our people will exercise no control. The new organization will not be subject to Parliament or to the Governor in Council; I would propose that at least it shall be subject to the control of the Railway Commission. For the reasons which I have given here in committee, I submit that this clause and the one following it are against the public interest. I propose to vote against them, and later to submit an amendment.

I think it will be agreed that there is a doubt as to whether we exercise control at the present time over the ocean freight rates of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. Perhaps we do, but if we do not it is possible for the Government of Canada to secure that control. Last session the Government introduced a Bill to that end; I do not know why it was not brought up this year and put into effect before the introduction of such legislation as this. I should like to ask any hon gentleman-the hon. member who has charge of the Bill (Mr. W. H. Sharpe) or the Minister of Railways-what disadvantage the Canadian Pacific Railway Company is subjected to at the present time by reason of the Canadian ownership of these steamships? Does any one suppose for a moment that by organizing a new company and having the bonds secured by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, the Canadian Pacific Railway Company can get money any cheaper than they can get it under their own name? No company can get money cheaper than the Canadian Pacific Railway Company; I imagine that even the Government of Canada cannot do it. Why, then, do they ask Parliament to-day to authorize the withdrawal of their ocean and coast steamships from the control of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company? Why do they ask Parliament to place this steamship service under the control of what my hon. friend (Mr. Maclean) calls a foreign company, and what I call a foreign company, because it will not be subject to the control of the Canadian people?
The coasting vessels at Prince Rupert and Vancouver would, under this legislation, also pass out of our control.

Yes, they are engaged in the coasting trade. This new company might as well be incorporated in Germany as in Great Britain, so far as our control of it is concerned. I ask again: under what

disability is the Canadian Pacific Railway Company labouring at the present time? Has Canada not treated them well? Have we not given them almost everything they asked for? Have we made any unfair or unreasonable exactions from them in the past?
I will admit that they have given us good service. They are a big corporation; they have a big business, and they have conducted it, generally speaking, on good business principles. But has the company anything to complain of in respect of its treatment by the people of Canada or by the Government? I think it will be universally admitted that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company has absolutely nothing to complain of. What, then, are the grounds upon which they ask Parliament to have this steamship service withdrawn from the control of Canada, from the control of the Canadian Parliament, from the control of the Canadian people? There must be some reason.
They never have been under the control of Canada; they have been registered in England right along.

The minister says they have not been under Canadian control. But on every occasion upon which the Canadian Pacific Railway Company wanted money to buy boats or to acquire other' properties, they came to this Parliament for authority to issue stock; so that we have an indirect control, at any rate. Moreover, if the Prime Minister would reintroduce and have passed the legislation that he introduced last year, absolute control would be secured. In view of what has been done for the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, the people of Canada have a right to control its operations. What have the people done for the Canadian Pacific Railway Company? We built $32,000,000 or $33,000,000 worth of railway, and handed it over to them-for nothing. We gave them
25,000,000 acres of land-for nothing. We gave them other assistance and other bonuses to help the company along. And can it now be said that the people have no right to exercise any control over the doings of this company? Can it be said that all the money which the people assisted the Canadian Pacific Railway Company to raise was used in the building of the Canadian Pacific railway or its branch lines? Any one who would say that has a very superficial idea of the ramifications of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company as it exists to-day. I am speaking now of the operations of the company in Canada. Let us see what they control in addition to their

ocean and coast steamers and their Great lake fleet. They have a string of hotels from the Atlantic to the Pacific. They have lands given them by the people and lands purchased by themselves-lands which are now townsites, worth millions and tens of millions of dollars. The people of Canada put up part of the money with which these purchases were made; the Government of Canada gave them permission to issue bonds to secure the
5 p.m. money to buy these townsites and other properties. They have a large amount of money invested in smelters and in mines in British Columbia. The money that they put into these-industries was supplied partly by the capital this Parliament authorized the company to raise and partly by bonuses given them by the people of this country. Look at the timber they own at the present time. They are now asking that the steamship services only be separated from the company, but I have here an interview with Sir Thomas Shaughnessy, in which he intimates that they propose that all outside properties shall be eliminated from the control of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company proper. They have spent millions of dollars on irrigation lands. We granted them authority to sell securities to obtain money for that purpose; in a little while they will separate these properties also from the main company. Then they have telegraph lines, electric railways, express companies. The Hull Electric railway, which runs into Ottawa, is owned by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. In a short time, according to Sir Thomas Shaughnessy, the Canadian Pacific Railway Company will ask permission to withdraw all these outside interests from the control of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company proper. Do they propose at the same time to reduce the capital of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company? Not at all. The Canadian Pacific Railway Company are just a little afraid that possibly the Canadian Parliament may ultimately control their ocean freight rates, and they are taking steps to prevent this before the legislation of my right hon. friend the Prime Minister, introduced by his Government last year, is put into force. Shall we stand idly by and make no protest while that is being done?
How does the legislation of last year amending the Railway Act affect or conflict with this Bill?

Not being a lawyer, I probably do not understand the matter very well; but in a general and rough and ready

way, I think I understand this; and I think my right hon. friend the Prime Minister and the Minister of Railways must have understood it in the same way when they introduced the legislation giving power to the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada to supervise the securities that were issued by the railway companies. I think that w'ould go so far as to cover not only the issuing of the securities themselves but the guaranteeing of securities of any subsidiary company, and if it did not give such power the Act should be so amended as to give it. So I do not think we can get away from the fact that at the present time we are in the very good position of being able, in view of the legislation introduced by the Government last year, to have control of the capitalization and the securities issued by these different railway companies and other companies.
Let us see how it is going to affect those who have to pay the freight rates. The hon. member for South York (Mr. W. F. Maclean) has spoken of its effect on the western farmer. He never said truer words in his life. We talk about the disadvantage the war has been to everybody. So it has in many ways, but financially the war has been a godsend to the people of the West; and if it had not been for the high prices obtained for the last crop there would have been a much greater protest from the West against the passage of any legislation such as we are now considering than there has been. Let us see the position in which the western farmer will be when this legislation is passed. Prices are high now, everybody, particularly the Government, is urging on the farmer to go in for production and patriotism. Well they need not bother about the patriotism end, the farmers are as patriotic as they are; nor need they bother about the production. There is no occasion to tell the farmer, if he has a field ready to sow, to sow it, if he can get the seed.
But he has to get the seed.

In some cases he has to get the seed, but there is no need to lecture him on the growing of his crop or on patriotism. Let us suppose that this war ends sometime during the coming summer, as I think in all probability it will. Great Britain has a year's food on hand to-day. I have no doubt that France is in much the same position. These countries that are at war are not going on a margin of one or
two months' food supply, they have a huge supply of food products on hand and when the Dardanelles are opened in the course of a few weeks there will be an outlet for an immense amount of food supply and you will find that all the Allies will be well stocked up. Supposing the war ceases next fall, what will happen? Do you think the high prices will be maintained? Not for one moment, there will be a slump in the prices of food products, and a big slump. Then where will the farmer be? I make the statement without fear of contradiction that to-day it cost from 6 cents to 8 cents a bushel more to take wheat from Fort William to Montreal than it did three or four years ago. Why?
