The railroads are not charging more to bring it to Fort William, there has not been very much increase in freight rates on the Great Lakes; the great bulk of the increase has been on the ocean end. The ocean freight rates have been increased so that, as I say, there is now a difference of from 6 to 8 cents a bushel.
May I point out that before reaching the sea, on the Atlantic seaboard, flour that used to sell in my constituency at from $5.75 to $6 a barrel is now selling at $8 and $8.50 a- barrel.
That has nothing to do with the question we are now discussing.
I am trying to say that regardless of the ocean rates there has oeen an unjustifiable increase in the price of flour in Canada.
So much the worse.

I do not think it has anything to do with the question I am discussing; but I shall give the answer to my hon. friend's question. The big milling companies bought wheat last Fall, millions and tens of millions of bushels, at 80 cents and 90 cents a bushel, and later on they perhaps bought it at a $1 a bushel. Owing to manipulation, to a certain extent, but partly to the big demand in European countries, not only the countries at war but those that expected that they would be drawn into the war, putting in huge supplies of wheat, the price went from $1 up to $1.50 and $1.60 a bushel, and the mills are therefore charging for .flour which they grind from wheat which cost them less than $1 a bushel, the price they would charge if they had paid $1.50

and $1.60 a bushel. That accounts for the increase in the price.
The enhanced price does, not go to the farmers in the West.

A great deal did not, because the large proportion of the crop had been sold before the 1st of January last year, so the farmers did not get the advantage of the whole increase in price. The great bulk of the crop was sold before the price reached $1.50 a bushel. Many farmers thought that when wheat got to 9Q cents or $1 a bushel it was a good price, and it was, and they sold for that good price. But I do not think that argument has much to do with the question that we are now discussing. The freight rates have been increased, and that increase has taken place partly for transportation before the produce reaches the ocean, but largely for carriage on the ocean.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: How does the hon. member account for the fact that since this war broke out, in England freight rates have increased more than 100 per cent ?
That has nothing to do with the question, and the only way I can account for it is that the Government of Great Britain had commandeered hundreds of vessels that were engaged in carrying freight.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I am speaking of the railroad freight rates in Great Britain.

Because I think in England they ane not a bit better than we are; and when the railroad magnates think they see a good chance to do the people oy extra freight Tates they have probably taken advantage of it.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The Government took over the railroads as soon as the war broke out.

I do not know anything about freight rates in England, and I do not care what they do there. 'If they do wrong there that is no -reason and no excuse for doing wrong in Canada, and I do not think my. hon. friend will say it is a good excuse. But here is a company under no disability whatever in Canada, coming to Parliament with -a very mild-looking couple of clauses in another Bill altogether, having nothing to do with ocean shipping; and with these two mild-looking clauses they propose to take out of the jurisdiction of Canada forever any possible

chance of having any say whatever in connection with ocean freight rates. I say there is absolutely no justification for it. I -assume that the Prime Minister was in earnest when he introduced his legislation last year, providing for the regulation of ocean freight rates. That legislation has not yet come into effect; it is still before Parliament; and if, before that legislation is put in force, he -allows the Canadian Pacific railway to withdraw from the scope of that legislation a l-ar-ge portion of their -assets, then he will be responsible for something that should not be done and for which the Government will be held strictly to account.
The farmer in Canada has got to the limit of what he can stand. If it had not been for the higher prices obtained this year on account of the war, not a dollar would have been made out or last year's crop, even by those who had a good crop. And remember how the burdens of the farmer are to be increased this session. Here are the railroads clamouring before the Railway Commission for an increase in freight rates. They say the increase will not apply west of Port Arthur; but how can it be said that the West will not be affected by the increased rate from Port Arthur down to the Atlantic, when our western wheat goes over that line, and when a lot of the stuff we use in the West is drawn over that line from the East? But that is not all. It is proposed to increase the cost of producing wheat to a very large extent. The Government is increasing the cost of everything the farmer uses in producing his wheat. The Railway Board is likely to increase the freight rates, I understand, and now we have the Canadian Pacific railway trying to withdraw their steamships from the control of this Parliament, so that they can do any mortal thing they like in the way of increasing freight rates on the ocean.

How can it hurt the farmer of the West? The Bill is for the purpose of strengthening the Canadian Pacific Railway in their competition on the Seas. For the Canadian Pacific Railway has not a monopoly of ocean traffic; it has to compete with the steamship companies of Great Britain and of the United States and of foreign countries. This Bill will strengthen the owner of Canadian vessels in his competition with other steamship companies.

What disability is the
company under at present?

As I understand it,
they want to be able to conduct their business in a business-like way. I do not want to interject an argument into my hon. friend's speech; but it strikes me that this Bill is very much in the interests of the people of Canada, because it keeps everything that the commission has control over limited to the seaboard. The companies cannot mix their rates as partly land and partly ocean, which might be done if they were not separate companies. I cannot see anything in this Bill except the strengthening of the Canadian Pacific Steamships in their competition with steamship lines of other companies of foreign nations. I do not see how that can hurt the Canadian farmer or the eastern or western citizen.

The Canadian Pacific
railway is not conducting its ocean business in a businesslike way, simply because it is a branch of the main company.
It is not a branch of the railway at all. The whole argument of my hon. friend is based on a fiction. -

It is a part of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. The boats were secured by the money of the Canadian Pacific railway. Where else was the money obtained? This proposal, that the Canadian Pacific railway should have power to guarantee the securities of this new company, will not relieve'the Canadian Pacific railway in the slightest degree, except in this sense: it will relieve them for the future from control by the Parliament of Canada. In view of the fact that the legislation before us will have the effect of enabling the Canadian Pacific railway to enter into combines and to secure a greater monopoly of ocean traffic than they now have, and in view of the legislation introduced by the Government last year, surely it would be the part of wisdom for this House to say: We will let this Bill stand for a year, until the Prime Minister makes good the legislation introduced last year. If we do that we shall not be hurting the Canadian Pacific railway. They have gone on for years with their ocean service as a branch of or as a part of their main company; they have not suffered at all, and they are not suffering to-day. They have any amount of money in their treasury, and if they have not, they can get it just as readily through the present company as through the proposed new company. So we should be imposing no hardship whatever on the Canadian Pacific railway by delaying this Bill. What good rea' 47
son can be brought against allowing the Bill to stand? It is quite possible I may be absolutely wrong in the views I hold on this subject, but I think it would be best for the Bill to stand until next session when, during the recess we shall have had an opportunity of learning more about it. Surely that is not asking too mmjh, especially when there is a great possibility that its enactment may be to the detriment of the people who use the railway and the ocean service of the Canadian Pacific railway. Take my own constituency, absolutely an agricultural constituency, practically a wheat-growing constituency. The fact that it costs our farmers drom 6 to 8 cents a bushel more than it did a year ago to send wheat to the Old Country means that every farmer of the West is being deprived of that 6 or 8 cents a bushel, and when the war is over they will not be able to stand these increased rates. This war will have one effect, and hon. gentlemen opposite, and the Government especially, should not lose sight of it. In the West to-day to one farm occupied you will find two farms empty, in township after township; and that is not in the drouth-stricken area, but in districts that had a good crop last year. How is that? Simply because the farmer is finding it harder every year to make a living.

Low prices and
high freights.
Narrow markets.

And combines, monopolies, high freight rates, and the tariff. It means that you are going to drive the farmers from the land, not by hundreds, but by thousands. I may be wrong in thinking that this legislation will have that effect. But I think the Canadian Pacific railway is no better than another company; it is just as ready as the Grand Trunk or the Canadian Northern railway or any other steamship company to take the last cent from the farmer in freight rates. The farmers have not been able in the past to stand the high rates, and many of them have been driven off the farms. I fear that this legislation will have the effect of driving thousands and thousands of our farmers off the land. It makes me tired to hear this propaganda of getting people back to the land. That is beginning at the wrong end. What is wanted is legislation that will enable the farmer who is on the land to stay there. If you enable the farmers to stay on the



land, you do not have to bother about a propaganda to get them tb go back to the land. There are thousands of people living in cities who* would be glad to go on the land if they felt .they could make a living from the land. But you are going the wrong way about it by introducing this legislation in view of, the fact that the Government brought down legislation dealing partly with this question last year. I would suggest that this whole matter be left over until another session. Then we could take up the matter and thresh it out on its merits.
Suppose the Government did control this steamship company and did control the rates, what benefit would it be? Where would we benefit from it?
According to the argument of my hon. friend, we might better dissolve the Railway Commission. Has it been of no advantage to have the Railway Commission controlling rates? I think it has.
But they have controlled them under the system of allowing them to pay, have they not? They have not fixed railway rates at less than it paid the railways to carry the stuff?

Three or four years ago the ocean companies were charging very much lower rates than they are at the present time, and we did not hear of any great difficulties among the ocean steamship companies. They were declaring good dividends until some men got together in New York and London, merged these companies and issued a large amount of watered stock upon which they have not been able to pay dividends. But there is no doubt that on the actual amount of money invested in these steamsihip companies they were making good returns. .
Were they making money in these companies?
They were paying dividends.
Then why did they sell? If you were making money out of a corporation, would you sell out?
I would not hesitate to sell if I were making money out of it.

May I ask if this Bill stands over until the Government bring down the measure that was introduced last session, would not that measure apply to

all steamship companies as well as to the Canadian Pacific railway?

I think so. I think that would be the advantage of having this legislation passed instead of discriminating against other companies by giving special advantages to the Canadian Pacific railway. If this Bill is passed this session, and next session the right hon. the Prime Minister brings down and passes the legislation to which my hon. friend has referred, there may be disabilities as against other companies that he has exempted this company from.

This Bill would not have any such effect, because if this Parliament has power to pass the legislation which was proposed at the last session applying to all steamship lines, the legislation would apply equally to the Canadian Pacific Ocean Services Limited. In our desire to try and get rates reduced, and it is a very laudable desire and one in regard to which my hon. friend from Assiniboia has always proved himself to be the friend of the western producers, we ought not to be unfair to the Canadian Pacific Railway simply because it is a great and successful company which, as has been said by the hon. member for South York (Mr. Maclean), has done so much for the development of Canada and, indeed, whose development and prosperity have been wrapped up to a great extent with the prosperity and development of our country. Parliament at this session has given the Grand Trunk Railway Company identically the same powers as those which are asked for by the Canadian Pacific railway.	, J gft
The Bill was passed on the same day as this Bill was held up.
The powers are exactly the same.

Will my hon.
friend read them?

They are in different
language, but the effect is exactly the same.
Read them, please.

The directors of the company may from time to time, as often as they deem expedient and in such manner and upon such terms as may be mutually agreed upon-
The very language to which my hon. friend takes exception in this case.

*-make advances to or assist any company, now or hereafter incorporated, of which the capital stock issued and outstanding, or a controlling amount thereof, is now or may at the time of any such advances or assistance be held by or in the name of, or for the benefit of the company, and may acquire, hold, guarantee,-
That is the word to which my hon. friend takes such strong exception.
Yes.

-guarantee, pledge, sell or otherwise dispose of shares, bonds, debentures or other securities of any such company and for any such purposes may use the proceeds of any class of stock heretofore or hereafter issued by the Company, and upon the acquisition of any such shares, bonds, debentures or other securities may exercise all the powers of holders thereof and receive any dividends or interest paid thereon.
Under that section the Grand Trunk Pacific, or the Grand Trunk Railway Company, could to-morrow organize lines oi steamships both on the Atlantic and the Pacific, put them under the name of another company and guarantee the stock and other securities of that subsidiary company. Then we find that the Canadian Northern Railway Company have segregated their steamship line from the railway; the steamships are owned by the -Canadian Northern Railway Company, but held in the name of The Canadian Northern Steamships, Limited, and owned in the same way as it is proposed that this company may own the steamships of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. We ought not to discriminate against the Canadian Pacific Railway simply because it is a great company and has done so much for Canada, while giving the same powers exactly to the Grand Trunk Railway Company and recognizing the right of the Canadian Northern Railway Company to have the same powers when they organized the Canadian Northern Steamships Limited.
Mr. SAM. SHARPE: Did not this Parliament at the last session, when granting the loan to the Canadian Northern Railway Company, combine the Canadian Northern Steamship Company with the Canadian Northern Railway Company proper, and are we not doing exactly the opposite in this case?

At the last session the separate existence of the Canadian Northern Steamships Company Limited was not wiped out, but the company was connected as a steamship company the same as all other 47i
subsidiary companies with the Canadian Northern Railway Company, and all we did was to require that they should be merged together in the sense of all the securities which were to be issued being chargeable upon the mortgage. The reason was that as the Government was guaranteeing the bonds of the company to the amount of $45,000,000 it required that all the assets of the Canadian Northern Railway Company and of the subsidiary companies, some twenty or more in number-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Should be put in a convenient form for giving security.

Yes, should be covered by the securities. The Canadian Northern Steamship Lines maintained their identity just the same as the twenty or more subsidiary companies continued their identity. I remember a very strong argument was urged for preserving the identities of these companies at that time. If Parliament has the power to regulate the rates of ocean steamships, it will have the same power after this Bill passes to regulate the rates of the Canadian Pacific Ocean Services Limited as it will have in regard to the Donaldson line, the White Star line, the Allan line, the Beaver line and all those various lines of steamships now crossing the Atlantic. Surely we ought not to discriminate as against one railway company in respect to its steamships, and not control the rates exacted by the other lines. If Parliament can pass a law such as is proposed, there is nothing in the Bill now before the House to prevent a statute after it is passed being effective as against the lines of the Canadian Pacific Oceean Services Limited just as much as in respect to any other lines of steamers. In regard to the right of the Canadian Pacific Railway to be allowed to do what they seek power to do, I asked my hon. friend from South York as to whether or not the Canadian Pacific Railway Company was ever obliged by statute to establish steamship lines. I thought that might have an important bearing upon the consideration of this Bill. He has admitted, and I have no doubt that it is the case, that there is no obligation, that there never has been any obligation, on the part of the Canadian Pacific Railway to establish or operate steamships on either the Atlantic or the Pacific. There is nothing to prevent that company, without any violation of its charter and obligation to the Canadian people, disposing of all its steamship lines to-morrow.

Has it not
created a public service under that original charter ?

It created it through money earned by the railway, I presume, and which otherwise would have been distributed to its stock-holders. I presume that certain earnings of the Canadian Pacific railway, instead of being distributed to its stock-holders, have been used for the acquisition of these steamships. I can understand that as a matter of purely domestic arrangement within itself, it may be very convenient for the Canadian Pacific railway to organize a separate company, just as the Canadian Northern has done, to operate its steamship lines. My hon. friend (Mr. W. F. Maclean) talks of segregating the assets, and he says the Canadian Pacific railway may come here by and by to separate the hotel system from the railway. What of it; we have allowed that to be done by the Grand Trunk company. This magnificent hotel, the Chateau Hotel at Ottawa, is not owned by the railway company, but by what is known as the Ottawa Terminals Company. The hotels at Edmonton, Regina, Prince Rupert, and in the Rocky mountains, are owned, as I understand it, by the Grand Trunk Pacific Development Company, and not one of them by the railway company. Where would be the harm and who would object if the Canadian Pacific Railway to-morrow were to organize a great hotel company, in which would be vested these various hotels, so that they would be managed separately from the railway company ?
If these hotels are in the railway proposition now, and they do segregate them, do they propose to cancel the capitalization which now represents them in the capitalization of the eompdny ?
Let me ask my hon. friend what would happen if they sold these hotels outright ?
They should put the money represented by them into the capitalization. ^

I presume the money
would go into the treasury and if Parliament has any control over it well and good. But undoubtedly they have the power to sell such of their property, outside- of their railway, as they think it advisable to dispose of. The Canadian Pacific Railway

Company could to-morrow sell all their steamers, and they could to-morrow sell all their hotels. Where is the objection from the public standpoint to they themselves organizing a separate company to manage these steamships or to manage the hotels? Wherein is the objection to their having the power to guarantee the securities of the subsidiary companies, so that the money may be raised at a lower rate in the markets of the world, and thereby the charges upon the public less than if the subsidiary companies were obliged to pay a higher rate of interest upon the borrowed moneys. I can see no reason at all which would induce me to vote against the Bill, which I believe is entirely one of domestic concern for the Canadian Pacific Railway.
There is another consideration for those of us who are interested in Canadian ports-I suppose all members of this House are interested in Canadian ports, although some may be interested more than others because 'of local circumstances and considerations- and it is that we should not impose disabilities upon any railway company in respect to its line of steamers which would have the slightest effect in inducing it to discriminate against Canadian ports, or to disregard the business of Canadian ports and attempt to carry the trade through the ports of the United States. Suppose the Grand Trunk Railway Company were to come to-morrow to get authority to organize a great line of steamers upon the Atlantic, and to organize a subsidiary company for the purpose of owning and managing these steamers, and have power to the parent company to guarantee their bonds. Surely we would give that authority at once. We want to make Canadian ports favourite ports for ocean business. If we were to impose disabilities upon the Canadian Pacific Railway, and discriminate against them as compared with other lines of railway owning steamships, one could very well understand what might happen. They might dispose of their steamers altogether to companies in which they wrould have no interest and over which they would have no control, and instead of preserving that business to Canadian ports we might be doing very serious injury to the trade of these ports. I say, encourage by all means possible the enlargement of the ocean fleets of the Canadian Pacific Railway, and if they want it-and they would not come to Parliament unless they thought it would be an advantage to them in their financial operations and in the operation of their steamship lines-I say by all means

give them the widest possible powers. Then, if we can pass a general law applicable to all steamship companies, which would enable Parliament or the Railway Commission to control the rates, by all means pass it and make it applicable to all steamship lines as well as to the steamers of the Canadian Pacific railway.
Mr. SAM. SHARPE (North Ontario): It seems to me that Parliament is attempting to do this session exactly the opposite of what it did last session in the4case of the Canadian Northern Railway Company. Last session we spent a great deal of time to compel the Canadian Northern Railway to combine its various companies and various assets into such a corporation as would enable it to give certain securities to this Parliament for advances made. In the case of the Canadian Pacific Railway now, we are apparently dismembering the corporation, and separating it and weakening it, and, to a certain extent, losing the control which Parliament has at present over it. I was present in the Railway Committee, and I listened with a great deal of interest to the discussion that took place there, and I am free to say that I was greatly impressed by the argument presented by the hon. member for South York (Mr. W. F. Maclean). The Canadian Pacific Railway is a mighty corporation; it has been built up with the great assistance of the Canadian people, who gave them 25,000,000 acres of land and $25,000,000 in money. We are all proud of the great enterprise, and no person wants to hamper it in any shape or form. In any remarks I may. make I wish it to be understood that I have no hostility whatever to the Canadian Pacific Railway. I have always been friendly to the company, and I like to see it prosper as the country prospers, but it seems to me that every member who registers his vote in favour of this proposition is voting against the public interest of this country. We are now in practically what is a war session, and it was understood that no important legislation would be enacted outside of war measures, and the railway company will not be hampered if this legislation rest for a year or so, in order that Parliament may become seized of all its ramifications.
I moved in the Railway Committee that these two clauses should be referred to the Railway Board. We have there an expert body in Mr. DTayton and his associates. Mr. Drayton made a trip to the old country for the purpose of investigating these ocean rates and this very question, and I moved
in the Railway Committee that the whole subject be submitted to him, in order that he might if necessary suggest safeguards in connection with this, legislation. If it is dangerous legislation we should have expert opinion on it. It was said in the Railway Committee that there was no precedent for any such thing, but I remember*two or three years ago in the Private Bills Committee, when a water-power Bill came up for consideration, I moved that it' be referred to the Conservation Commission, headed by Sir Clifford Sifton, and that motion was carried. Sir Clifford Sifton and his expert associates went into the merits of the Bill, with the result that they reported against nine of the fifteen clauses. Why should we be paying these expensive commissions, if we cannot use them when we desire to? If these commissions can give us any assistance or any advice to protect the public, why should we not get it from them? Why should we be opposed to submitting this Bill to the Railway Commission to see if they cannot arrange proper safeguards to regulate ocean freight rates? The sense of the committee was against adopting my motion, and it did not pass.
There is no question to my mind but that a most important thing in a young and progressive country like ours, is to have favourable freight rates. That is important, not only to the western farmer but to the Ontario farmers and the Canadian farmer generally. We are shipping cattle and hogs and farm produce in Ontario, and these ocean shipping combines are sucking the life-blood out of the Canadian producer. We must not confess our inability and impotence to provide a remedy. We should grasp the question and devise means whereby we can have control over these ocean rates, and we should not be in too great hurry to pass this legislation. Why not consider it carefully and let the matter come up at a future session of Parliament? The member for South York pointed out that we are allowing the Canadian Pacific Railway to guarantee the bonds of a foreign corporation, iand we are facilitating them in getting away from the control of this Parliament and of the Railway Board. An article on the front page of Saturday Night, March 6, 1915, discussed the question of freight rates, and it is startling to hear of the enoTmous and staggering increases that have taken place in ocean freight rates during the past year. Judge J. W. Alexander, Chairman of the United States Committee on Merchant Mar-

ine and Fisheries, in a recent article in defence of that Government's Ship Purchase Bill, which it may be stated has been practically talked to death, and will probably be heard from no more, gives some astonishing figures in connection with this subject.
The article is as follows:
The company has done that now.
Has ' the company submitted itself to the jurisdiction of the Railway Board?
Yes.
Two years ago.

That is all the more reason why the proposed amendment should be accepted. We all know that the Railway Board has done excellent work. If we have confidence in the Railway Board, then why refuse the amendment of the hon. member for South York (Mr. Maclean) ? The hon. member does not say: This shall not be done. He simply says: It shall be done by a board in which we have the greatest confidence. We have confidence in the Railway Board, which is not going to impose onerous conditions upon the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. It will deal with that company fairly; it will not impose conditions upon the company that will drive it to American ports. Why should we refuse a reasonable amendment which provides that these transfers shall be made and the proceeds of these sales shall be employed only for such purposes and upon such terms as the Railway Board shall designate? That is a very reasonable proposition.

My hon. friend the member for Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff) asked: What disability will the Canadian Pacific Railway be under if it is allowed to remain just as it is to-day? The steamship lines were built up out of the earnings of the company. The people of Canada paid for them. Why do we not compel the company to register its ships under Canadian register? The only excuse offered to the Railway Committee by Mr. Beatty, counsel for the Canadian Pacific Railway, was that-it would simplify bookkeeping to transfer the ships. With all respect to that gentleman, I think that is an absurd reason. It is no reason for this Parliament to allow such a radical change to take place as regards the policy of the Canadian Pacific Railway. If it is only to simplify bookkeeping, we should stay our hands, because we know that, with all the ramifications of a company like the Canadian Pacific Railway, it has a proper system of bookkeeping. That is no excuse to offer to reasonable men legislating in the interest of the people of Canada.
This legislation is aiming to do just the opposite of what we were doing before. When we wanted the Canadian Northern Railway securities, we spent days and weeks compelling the Canadian Northern to form one holding company into which to put all its assets. We wanted it to put all its assets into one basket, so that we would know what they were. In this case we are allowing the Canadian Pacific Railway to divide itself up into several companies, and we are weakening the control that we should have oveT it. I trust that the amendment of the hon. member for South York will receive endorsation at the hands of hon. members.
I did not hear the hon. member for South York move any amendment to the Bill.
We are on section 4.
My amendment is on the Votes and Proceedings.
It has not been moved yet.
It will be moved at the proper time.

The hon. member proposed his amendment before the Railway Committee. If sections 4 and 5 contain all the atrocious things the hon. member says they do contain, I would have no hesitation in voting against the passage of those two
sections. I do not see, however, that the hon. member for South York or the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff) or the hon. member for North Ontario (Mr. Sharpe) have shown us that any of the things will happen which they say are going to happen by the passage of this Bill. When this Bill came before the committee, section 3 read as follows:
The company may sell, lease or charter any steam or other vessels of the company to the Canadian Pacific Ocean Services, Limited, an incorporated company, or to any other incorporated company.
That gave the Canadian Pacific Railway Company power to sell, lease or charter its boats on the Great Lakes. It was immediately seen that this matter took the boats on the Great Lakes and the inland boats of the railway company away from the jurisdiction of the Railway Board under which they are at present. The proposal was at once made in the committee that an amendment should be put in as follows:
Excepting the inland river and lake boats of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company.
The Canadian Pacific Railway Company did not oppose that amendment, and this shows their recognition of the fact that the ocean liners of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company are not and never were under the jurisdiction of the Board of Railway Commissioners. This legislation, therefore, does not attempt to put these services outside the jurisdiction of the Board of Railway Commissioners. The Canadian Pacific Railway Company may sell, lease or charter their boats, or may dispose of them in any way they may desire, and they ask that in doing so they may guarantee the stock of the Canadian Pacific Ocean Services Company or any other incorporated body which may purchase or acquire those boats. Is that an unheard-of thing? Certainly not; we are doing it every day. We are doing it in connection with all railway companies; why should we not do it in connection with the Canadian Pacific Railway Company? The new company is paying for these boats not by handing gold to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, but by means of bonds and securities. It is provided that the company may subscribe for, purchase, take, acquire, hold, guarantee. Is there anything unbusinesslike in that? Is there anything in this legislation which will prevent the Board of Railway Commissioners from exercising any control of ocean rates which they do not exercise at the present time? The hon. member for South York spent two

days in the Railway Committee and an hour in the House to-day arguing this point; he is as clear about it now as hfe was then, and that is as clear as mud. It is recognized by the best legal talent in Canada that the Board of Railway Commissioners have no jurisdiction over ocean freights at the present time; how in the world can this proposed legislation take away from them that which they have not?
At six o'clock the Committee took recess.
The Committee resumed at 8 o'clock.

It has been suggested
that one way in which this Government could make the' Canadian Pacific Railway subject itself in the way of giving the Railway Board jurisdiction over its freight rates -would be to compel the Canadian Pacific Railway to have its boats registered in Canada. I believe that if that were done it would result in the ocean liners controlled by the Canadian Pacific Railway and other companies plying to ports in the United States. I do not think that would be to the advantage of the people of Canada, much less to the farmers of the West who have grain to ship across the Atlantic. The member for South York (Mr. W. F. Maclean) said that this legislation would frustrate or defeat the object this Parliament had some years ago in incorporating this company and assisting it financially. I fail to follow him there. He cited a clause of the Act of incorporation which said that the Canadian Pacific railway should continue to.be operated as a first-class railway. I fail to see how, if this legislation passed and the Canadian Pacific Railway was allowed to lease or sell or charter their boats to an independent or subsidiary company, that would in any way interfere with the line continuing to be operated as a first-class railway. If there were anything in this Act which would be to the disadvantage of the farmers of the West or to any class or portion of the people of Canada, I do not think this committee would for an instant think of passing the Bill. How is the farmer going to be affected? The farmer in the West at the present time may appeal to the Railway Board, in so far as transcontinental freight rates are concerned. The farmer in the West is not in a position to appeal to the Railway Board in so far as ocean freight rates are concerned because the Railway Board has no jurisdiction and does not pretend to take to itself jurisdiction over ocean freight ratet at the present time. The only trouble

and the real difficulty that was in the Bill has been removed by the amendment made in the Railway Committee to clause 4, excluding from the operations of that clause the inland boats of the Canadian Pacific railway, so that it cannot dispose of them to a subsidiary company. The whole thing appears to me to be a business-like transaction. I do not believe that the Canadian Pacific Railway has in view the undoing of the farmers of the West or of any portion of the population of Canada. The Canadian Pacific Railway are running this road as a money maker like others and in running it they must give a fair measure of justice to the people of Canada. If they do not this Parliament is here to make them do so. If they attempt to raise transcontinental rates we will have recourse to the Railway Board; but I do not think there is much danger of such an abuse in view of the fact that they now have two transcontinental lines competing with them. My friend from South York is reading into these clauses things which the clauses do not contain. I am afraid he is gifted, if you can call it a gift, like one or two of the clans of the Highlands, with second sight and can see things nobody else can. There would be a great deal in his contention, everything that he is arguing for, if our Railway Board to-day had jurisdiction over ocean rates. They have not that jurisdiction, and therefore -we are not giving to the Canadian Pacific Railway any privilege which they Iiave not now, with the possible exception of guaranteeing the bonds of this subsidiary company.

Section agreed to.
On section 5:
The company may subscribe for, purchase, take, acquire, hold, guarantee, pledge and dispose qf shares, bonds and other securities of the Canadian Pacific Ocean Services, Limited, and of any other company to which the steam or other' vessels of the company may be sold, leased or chartered.

This is the clause that authorizes the Canadian Pacific Railway to endorse all this capitalization of the proposed new company. It is said that we have no jurisdiction over ocean rates or over this company. We have jurisdiction, I think, over ocean rates, certainly it has not been proved to me that we have not, but we have jurisdiction over the Canadian Pacific Railway, and they are here to-day as suppliants. The history of progressive legislation in Great Britain, in this country, in every country, is that grievances have been rectified when the persons who have acted unfairly have appeared before the

legislature as suppliants. The Canadian Pacific Railway is here to-day as a suppliant. It has imposed most unfair charges upon the people of the Canadian West for ocean transportation. It has done this because it entered into a combine on the north Atlantic; and it proposes now to make a still greater combine, and we have the company now under our legislative control, and it is proposed by this legislation that we should part with that jurisdiction and permit them to endorse any capitalization in connection with outside companies.
What are we letting them out of in this Bill?

I am asking that we shall keep them under control, that we shall say they must not endorse the bonds of this company without the consent of Parliament and of the Railway Commission of Canada. That is my proposal, and that is the thing that I wish to see adopted. Why should we say that we have no power, and let the company do what it likes with the credit we gave to it and allowed it to build up to its present position? It should not be permitted to lend this credit to another company. And grant that we gave permission to the Grand Trunk, as has been said, then we did wrong. I was in the committee the other day when that was up.

You never said a
word.
Perhaps not. The hon. gentleman did not.
I fixed the Bill up.

My great crime is that I do not watch everything; and if I try to watch one thing I am inconsistent. Probably the worst vice one can have is inconsistency. And then they say you are irrelevant, illogical, or the draughtsmanship is bad, as some of the lawyers say when you draw up an amendment. But Parliament never achieved any reforms without taking advantage of what it already possessed. We can secure a great deal in the public interest if we keep the capitalization of this railway under the control of Parliament or of the Railway Board. I have been through all this, and heard these charges of irrelevant and illogical argument, and of your statement being as clear as mud, and all those other polite things. And then the things you meet on the street. I could not go down the street to-night without having somebody say to me: "Oh, did you get that off?"-as if I was loaded with bile and
wanted to get it off. I went through all this in connection with the regulation of express charges in this country. The Minister of Justice and the man who aspired to that position told me that I was most illogical, that my draughtsmanship was bad, and that the jurisdiction did not apply. They have tried to keep express companies out of our jurisdiction, but they are now in it. Lawyers in this House would say: Oh, you have no jurisdiction over an express company, because it owns a boat service on the lake, or because some of the goods are carried by stage; and for a while the railways said we had no jurisdiction over the freights on inland waters in this country. But we have the jurisdiction now; we have acquired it in some way, but we should never have acquired it if we had confessed that we had no jurisdiction. We have some jurisdiction over the Canadian Pacific Railway in regard to freight rates. We have sent the Minister of Trade and Commerce on a commission to ascertain just what our jurisdiction is. But it does not do to confess you have no jurisdiction.
The argument of the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) was practically: Oh, you are making fish of one and flesh of the other. Now, I may be inconsistent; we all may be; but a progressive measure has never been put on the statute book in order to cure some grievance or to improve a certain condition, which did not do some injustice in some way to somebody. That is how reforms work out. They do not work out by clear-cut logical statements, but by Parliament trying to attain something. Reform is worked out by judges bending the law in the line it is supposed to move, ox-ought to move. There is always some injustice and some irregularity, but eventually you get progress. From my experience in Parliament I should say that the way to get reform-and it is a way that seems to be more disapproved than any other-is to follow the good old English method. When we have a corporation here as a suppliant for increased powers-and we have them every yeai

we should say to them:	If
you want relief we are going to examine your character; if you are asking for relief in regard to ocean steamship rates, why are you in the North Atlantic combine? Why will you not submit your rates to us? If we followed that method we should be constantly progressing, and should get legislation in the public interest. I do not care how irrelevant the argument may be, or what it may lack in clearness, but I say we should not abandon our position and

give this railway unlimited power to use its credit for the benefit of a steamship company outside the jurisdiction of Canada.
Are the Canadian Pacific Railway now in the North Atlantic combine?

I do not know; they
were in it as big as could be.

Was it not proved at
the investigation in the United States last summer that the Canadian Pacific Railway were not in the combine?
They have been in the combine, and have led the combine; just as they own the Allan line to-day and profess not to own it.

I understood they were
proved not to be in the combine.

It has not been proved. They have been in the combine; they are in it now; they are directing the North Atlantic combine, and are going to direct it more when they have this legislation. It is against the public interests that they should be given this power to guarantee the securities of a company outside of our control. They are under our control now and we should say to them: If you are going to use this power, you must use it subject to the approval of the Railway Commission of this country, as laid down in the Government Bill of last session and in the proposed amendment I have on the Order Paper this year.

The hon. member for
South York (Mr. W. F. Maclean) has made serious charges against the Canadian Pacific Railway. The Minister of Railways must know something about this, and I should., like to hear what he has to say about it. He has been looking over the Bill. He was in the Railway Committee the other day when the Bill was up.

speakeroldname: Hon. FRANK COCHRANE (Minister of Railways and Canals):
speechtext:
Everything seems
to have been discussed but the point of the Bill. I do not think there is any question of our power to pass legislation to control any ships that come within the three-mile limit or into our harbours. Would it do us any good to force this company to submit its rates to the Railway Commission or to the Government or to whomsoever it may be? It would only antagonize them, and drive them to other ports. I think there are three things which will help to get us 
lower ocean rates. First of all, we might make an international agreement with the United States in reference to a board; so that these ships could not be driven from Canadian ports to Boston, Portland or New York, which have all the time better rates than our own ports. There has been a little effort to bring that about. Another great thing is in regard to insurance. Insurance on vessels using Canadian ports is much higher than on vessels using American ports; that is a very serious thing, not only for ocean liners, but for tramp ships as well. Take Halifax or Quebec in the summer. These ports are then no more dangerous to approach or leave than Boston, for instance. In fact, I think either of the two ports I have mentioned is preferable to Boston. If we follow the advice of the hon. gentleman (Mr. W. I?. Maclean) and tell the Canadian Pacific Railway that we will not allow them to guarantee the bonds of the stock of this new company which they propose to create, this new company could get along without this help, but could not sell its stock or bonds in the market of the world as easily as it could if the Canadian Pacific Railway were behind it. The main reason for this legislation, as explained to me by ' the Canadian Pacific Railway, is because the British Government has commandeered nearly all their ships. That has caused freight rates to go up. They do not know when the boats will be given back to them, nor how many may be sunk before the war ends; so they have incorporated a company in England, and we all know how Lloyd George looks after companies there. They want to get these ships started at once; and the more ships we have on the Atlantic the lower the freights will be. Another great factor is the growth in our shipping, although it has not grown like American shipping. Again, there has not been much inducement to tramp steamers, which in my	opinion are a greater leveller
of	freights than	anything else.
I do not see any harm in the Bill. The views I have on this question are very much in line with those contained in the speech made by my hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Pugsley.) I think he laid down the case very clearly from all the different points of view. I think we would be only cutting off our noses to spite our faces if we accepted the amendment which has been given notice of. I do not agree that we have any control over ocean freight rates at the present time and I am of the opinion that the

Bill should go through. Some hon. gentlemen have talked all around this question, but they have not touched upon the real point at issue.

I think that my hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals {Mr. Cochrane) has come closer to the practical question in regard to the control of ocean freight rates than my hon. friend from South York (Mr. W. F. Maclean) did in considering this question. The problem of lower freight rates is one in which not only the farmer is interested but every man who is connected with the production of raw material or produce of any kind which he desires to send abroad. Every producer in every province of the Dominion who looks for a market in the Motherland, to which country our exports have increased very rapidly within the last ten years, is particularly interested in the problem of how to get these products carried to the old country as cheaply as possible and equally interested in getting what he purchases in Great Britain brought back to this country at the lowest possible figure. The question of what the freight rate upon these articles may be at any particular time does not depend upon any internal condition in this country. The whole thing is a problem of supply and demand and those men who have lived in the maritime provinces where we have had some connection with shipping interests know that within the last five years, indeed, down to a year and a half ago, and even later than that, the freight rates for our vessels that were owned and doing business there were at the verv lowest possible ebb. Within the last year the conditions have entirely changed and between
2,000	and 3,000 of the freight-carrying vessels of the world have been withdrawn from that service; the exact tonnage I do not know but I know that this large number of the vessels have been withdrawn in consequence of which a very much less tonnage is offering, or is available, for the	purpose	of	carrying ourproduce	to and	fro. The consequence is, just as in any other lines pf business in the world, that the cost of transportation has increased because there are fewer people in the business of transportation. There is another thing that hon. gentlemen who have spoken on this question seem to have forgotten and that is that Great Britain controls the carrying trade of the world upon the seas and the people in Great Britain are very much interested in getting all they can out of the n ships when the time for their harvest has arrived, so to speak. There is a greater demand for vessels now than at any time in the past, and the ship-owner of England, not being a special philanthropist, has taken advantage of the excessive demand for his tonnage just the same as a man in any other business would. My hon. friend comes in and says that because that is so, in this year of grace 1915, when the Canadian Pacific Railway asks us to pass a measure in the financial character of which there is nothing extraordinary, we should hold them up and not let this measure pass without stipulating that they cannot have anything to do with this new steamship company unless a clause is inserted in the Bill that freight rates shall be under the control of the Railway Commission.
I did not say that.
Is not that the whole purport of the hon. gentleman's argument upon the holding up of the Canadian Pacific Railway the question of the control of ocean freight rates?
No, I have never argued that.
Then what was my hon. friend talking about?
My argument was that the control of the securities of the company should come under the Railway Commission.
Who is going to regulate the freight rates?
I did not say;, we will find a way later on, but in the meantime do not let the control of our securities pass out of our hands.
I was listening to the hon. gentleman.

Listening to some of
your friends on the other side of the House.
My hon. friend is not going to disclaim his association with my hon. friend from Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff)?
I did not say it.
If he did not iterate and reiterate tlhait in the course of his speech I do not know what he was talking about in regard to ocean freight rates.
I did not say it.
Then, what did my hon. friend mean?

I meant what I have just said; I proposed that the Canadian Pacific Railway, should only give its endorsement to the securities of this other company after these securities had been approved by the Railway Commission.

What about ocean
freight rates?

You must ask those who dealt with that question. I said ocean freight rates were a grievance in this country and, in the meantime while they were a grievance, we should not let the control of ithe securities of the Canadian Pacific railway in connection with shipping pass out of our hands.

I think I am accurate in what I say. My hon. friend means that we should not give the Canadian Pacific Railway this legislation unless we do something in regard to ocean freight rates. We have power in this Parliament to pass legislation by which we shall say that the Board of Railway Commissioners, or some other board, should fix the rates to be inserted in .all bills of lading or charter parties in connection with the carrying of goods of different classifications, but the Minister of Railways and Canals has painted out that our jurisdiction in this matter would cease the moment any ship passed the three-mile limit or whenever we attempted to legislate beyond the confines of our country. But in the meantime, after putting that legislation into effect, there is this problem, that we have the United States to the south of us, and an exporter in Canada .at any point west of Quebec would divert his export trade to the American ports where there are no such limitations, no railway commissions, and ship his goods in that way. That is the way it would work out. That is the actual business result of it. At the same time we could not Dy any possibility control by our legislation here the freight rates which the English shipowner might ask the .shipper on the other side who wanted to ship his goods to Canada. Our lumbermen and our fishermen in the maritime provinces are quite as much interested in this question of freight rates as are producers of other classes in different parts of Canada. We are in this unfortunate position that, while Canada thirty years ago was at the very top of the list in the shippinv wotM when

she built her wooden vessels, she to-day has practically no vessels on the sea at all. Unfortunately our iron and steel industry (had not been advanced to that point, when our wooden vessels disappeared from the sea, that we could roll and combine steel plates into ships in the way in wfhich this work was done by the steel men of England who had a long lead on the people of any other country in the steel industry. To-day we have practically no Canadian merchant marine. As a consequence England's shipowners control this business, as to freight, as to transportation and as to all those questions of the sea and until you can make what might be called an international arrangement with England by which the English and Canadian Governments, or some joint commission to be appointed by both, would Ibave supervision over the question so that [DOT] you could make it work at both ends, any action by us Would be entirely inadequate and inoperative. In order to make that provision entirely effectual you would have to have an international arrangement between Great Britain and the United States by which the freight rates would be just the same in both countries. It seems to me that that is a fair statement of the actual business .conditions in regard to ocean freight rates. I would have liked to have heard from the bon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster), who has given this question his special attention, a statement of bis views upon this question because it is a most important one. The fault I have to find with imy hon. friend from Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff) is that the proposition as it is contained in the Order Paper in regard to this particular legislation in reference to ocean freight rates would be entirely inoperative and inadequate and there would be no sense in putting it on the statute books.
The question of the control of the capitalization of the company may open a very wide door. It is a question whether or not due publicity as to the assets of a company and other information given to the public with regard to any stock issue would *ot be quite as advantageous as to make it compulsory for any large enterprise to come to any particular board in this country to get a certificate of character. Suppose one of our large railway companies contemplating a bond or stock issue came to the Board of Railway Commissioners and succeeded in getting its approval of the right to issue the stock or bonds, it would be at once urged by investors abroad, in the event of any

failure on the part of the enterprise, that Canada through her properly constituted authorities had given a certificate of character to that enterprise and to the right to make that stock or bond issue, which misled the investor, and that might result in very great injury to the credit of the whole country in the future. On the other hand, if you have proper publicity in regard to the status of a company arranged for, then the investors would have to make their own investigations and take their own risk. It does seem to me that my hon. friend (Mr. W. F. Maclean) has not made any case which would entitle the House to say to a company that comes here with an ordinary business proposition, that it should be held up by the imposition of conditions which are entirely unnecessary and which would be inoperative and inadequate.

I wish to ask the Minister of Railways why the Canadian Pacific Railway Company should go to Great Britain for incorporation of the Canadian Ocean Services, Limited, instead of getting -incorporation in Canada?

The ships owned by them at present are registered in Great Britain, and I suppose whatever new ships they get will be acquired out of the funds guaranteed by the Canadian Pacific Railway. I do not know of any other reason.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
rates upon the ocean, or rates upon the land either. I cannot see that the forma-ticn-'of this new company would tend to facilitate a combine. The allegation has frequently been made here that the so-called Atlantic conference has tended towards the increase of rates; but so far as I can see, the establishment of any such conference in the future would not be in any way facilitated by the organization of a separate company in this case. As a matter of fact, in the United States they are forcing companies to do that which the Canadian Pacific railway desires to do now of its own accord. Legislation in the United States, and the decrees of the various commissions which [DOT]have been established in that country, have prevented one corporation from carrying on the business of a railway and the business of a steamship company at the same time. They have also prohibited railway companies in the United States from being interested in coal areas and carrying on the business of coal companies.
It would seem to me that if the steamship company proposed in this Bill had been organized years ago by capital provided by the Canadian Pacific railway or by those who were interested in that company, and if the proposal were made here to-day that it should be merged in the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, there would be even a louder cry than that which is put forward in opposition to this Bill now.
As to -weakening the Canadian Pacific Railway company, I cannot see that this Bill weakens it, and I think the company is pretty thoroughly able to safeguard its interests. As a matter of fact, there is not a great deal of change in the situation, as far as I understand it. The company up to the present time has invested a certain amount of its capital in the acquisition of steamship lines on the Atlantic and on the Pacific. Its ownership in those steamship lines would enable it to sell or dispose of them, so far as I understand the legal effect of the various Acts under which the Canadian Pacific Railway has acquired that ownership. What the Canadian Pacific Railway proposes to do is to organize a separate company, incorporated under the English Joint Stock Companies Act, with all the safeguards to which I have alluded, and it proposes that the ocean-carrying business of the Canadian Pacific Railway shall be transacted by this company and not by the parent company.

As far as control of rates is concerned, if the allegation be true that the profits from the ocean carrying business of the Canadian Pacific Railway are very large, the separation of that business in this distinct way is an advantage to the public rather than a disadvantage, because it will prevent any juggling with the receipts from the railway carriage and those from the ocean carriage, which might otherwise be possible. At all events, if it does not absolutely prevent that, it will make it more difficult. The Railway Commission would be able more distinctly to know that the profits of the ocean business were, as distinct from the profits of the railway company considered purely as a railway company.
The purpose of the Bill is almost altogether administrative, endeavouring to put the business of the Canadian Pacific Railway into a position in which it will be easier to carry on the ocean-carrying business as distinct from the la(nd-carriage business.
The only difference in the situation created by this Bill is this, namely that the Canadian Pacific Railway owns the steamships directly to-day, and that after this Bill has passed and after the steamships have been transferred to the new company which is to be organized, the Canadian Pacific Railway will own the steamships in effect although not directly, because it will hold the stock which represents those steamships. There will be no difference in substance although there will be a difference in administration.
It has been argued very strenuously that the stock may be distributed and divided amongst the shareholders of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. The Company cannot distribute its stock amongst the shareholders if it proposes, as I should imagine it would propose, to retain control of the ocean-carriage system, because if it distributes its stock amongst its shareholders, it will at once lose control, and the purpose which the company had when it embarked upon the business of transportation across the Atlantic and across the Pacific would cease to be effective. I would not therefore be inclined to attach importance to the idea that there would be any distribution of this stock, because the stock held by the Canadian Pacific Railway will represent the control which it must exercise, unless it proposes to go out of the ocean-carrying business.
So far as the guarantee of bonds is concerned, it is a very common thing amongst

railways-and I think it is a very common thing in the legislation which has been authorized by this Parliament for the Canadian Pacific Railway Company-to give to a major railway company-if I may use that expression-the power to guarantee the bonds of another company which it purchases or leases. It is precisely that principle which has been brought into this Bill,	namely, the purpose of	en-.
abling the Canadian Pacific Railway a very great corporation with very great assets, to guarantee the	bonds in
order that the money which is to be raised	for the purpose	of adding
to the steamship lines of the Canadian Pacific Railway may be raised at the lowest possible rates of interest. So far as that goes, it is manifestly a proposal in the interest not only of the whole enterprise but of the people of this country at large.

Would the value of the stock of the present shareholders of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company be decreased in any way by the transfer of the assets in the shape of ships, supposing the stock were given to persons who did not hold stock in the Canadian Pacific Railway?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I suppose the assets represented either by money or by stock would be in the Canadian Pacific Railway, and I do not see that it would affect the situation assuming that they were sold at their actual value. What impressed me was this, that it merely amounts to a change in the form of ownership. The Canadian Pacific Railway has direct ownership in those steamships under conditions as they are at present. After this proposal is carried out, that interest which it now possesses will be represented by stock held by the Canadian Pacific Railway in the new ocean steamship company. Do I make myself clear to my hon. friend?
Yes.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It does not affect the capitalization of the Canadian Pacific Railway, which remains the same; but that which was represented by the ownership of those vessels will, after this proposal is carried out, be represented by the stock held by the Canadian Pacific Railway in the company which owns the vessels. Therefore, I cannot see that there will be any actual or substantial change in the assets of the Canadian Pacific Railway which will be affected by this Bill.

I thought the question asked was: Are the rights of shareholders of Canadian Pacific Railway stock safeguarded under this legislation? Take, for example a man who owns 1,000 shares of Canadian Pacific Railway stock. After the ships are removed from the company, what does he get in lieu of that security; or is it in the power of the company to say: We will take the ships away from the assets, and we will leave you what you have? Will the new company give the Canadian Pacific Railway Company something in lieu of the consequent depreciation in the value of the stock ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Matters affecting the disposal or utilization of the assets of the company are left by the shareholders and directors. We are entitled to assume that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, when they sell these steamships, will get a reasonable price for them, and that that price will be represented either in money or in stock. I understand the proposal is that the price shall be realized in stock. The stock which the Canadian Pacific Railway Company will receive will represent the value of the vessels. Instead of a direct ownership, there will be an indirect ownership through the stock, but the value will be there just the same as it was before.

I think we all wish to be absolutely fair in matters of this kind, even in respect of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. I asked the hon. member for South York if the Canadian Pacific steamship services, as at present incorporated, are a part of the North Atlantic combine. He said that they are. My memory is most distinctly the opposite. Last year when the United States appointed a commission to investigate the North Atlantic combine, it was found, not only that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company had absolutely no connection with that combine, but that they were its chief competitor.
Hon. GEORGE P. GRAHAM: I am not inclined, like some hon. gentlemen, to chide the hon. member for South York (Mr. W. F. Maclean). I believe, with him, that we get no reforms of any consequence unless some one, begins to agitate. Sometimes agitations are made too soon; sometimes too strong; but no harm can result from genuine agitation which in the opinion of the agitator is necessary to effect some reform. I admit that some beneficial results have been accomplished in respect

to certain matters which the hon. member for South York first brought to the attention of the House, and I think that credit is due him for these results.
The hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff) did the natural thing when he requested the Government to insert in this Bill a clause providing for control of ocean freight rates, because the company, in a general way, promised to do something along that line. When I had the honour of being Minister of Railways and Canals and the late Justice Mabee was Chairman of the Board of Railway Commissioners, we conducted negotiations with the authorities in Great Britain looking to the inauguration of a scheme for the control of ocean freight rates. Justice Mabee expressed the view that we could control ocean freight rates, but, as has been pointed out by the Minister of Railways to-night, the control which we would exercise would be, in a large measure, unimportant; if Canada acted alone, the control exercised would not be sufficiently far-reaching. The present Solicitor General on one occasion took me to task for not getting the ocean freight rates under control, and h6 himself proposed to do it. The hon.
member for Assiniboia was 9 p.m. merely calling upon the Solicitor General to make good his promise, but it has not been a very easy task. I think the Government did send the present Chairman of the Board of Railway Commisioners to Great Britain to inquire into this matter. I do not know what information he gained, but I venture the assertion that he did not get much farther than I did. The reasons are quite apparent. This is a problem that cannot be solved by one country or by two countries; I am inclined to think that it could not be solved even if Great Britain, the United States and Canada were to unite in their efforts . to solve it. Great Britain owns a large proportion of the world's shipping, but many other countries as well are concerned. The negotiations which the late Government were conducting in this matter came to an abrupt termination. After it had been determined that it would be unnecessary and unprofitable to conduct any further correspondence, I discussed fairly and frankly with some of the authorities the prospects of carrying out such an arrangement. Some of the difficulties were made manifest, and are manifest now to those who understand the subject. Great Britain owns perhaps 90 per cent of the shipping cf the world, and

anything that we should do would be ineffective unless Great Britain co-operated with us. We could impose a license fee upon vessels landing goods at Canadian ports, but if we did that and some other country did not do so in respect of its own shipping, Canadian ports would be avoided. I discussed with men in authority the advisability of our co-operating with the United States in the matter, and it was agreed that our co-operation would solve the difficulty to a certain extent. But the chief difficulty which exists in connection with ocean or lake freights is not found in the control or management of railways. The Prime Minister made that quite clear. Any one who buys a ship can run it, but only the proprietors of a railway can manage a railway. Hon. gentlemen sometimes forget that if the Board of Railway Commissioners undertook to control freight rates on the ocean, they migjit be obliged, owing to changed conditions, to change rates as often as they had a sitting. Under regulations of the Board of Railway Commissioners, transportation companies are not allowed to carry freights at less than the rates agreed upon. To do so would be discrimination, for which a fine is imposed. Supposing a man wants to send a cargo to Canada from a point on the other side of the Atlantic or Pacific. In order to get a proper freight rate on that cargo, he wires to his agent on this side to see if he can get a return cargo, because ships, like railway trains, cannot gi"ve fair rates unless they get a cargo both ways. It quite frequently happens that the agent on this side can arrange for a return cargo at a very much lower rate than that which is usually charged, but, if the Railway Commission had previously fixed a certain freight rate, the steamship would be liable to a fine if the return cargo were carried at a lower rate. It is much more difficult to regulate ocean freight rates than it is to regulate railway freight rates. There are several difficulties in the way; I sympathize with the Government in that they are finding it not easy to do something in the accomplishment of *which their predecessors did not exactly succeed.
Public ownership of steamships would solve the difficulty.

Perhaps public ownership of steamships would do it, 'but that is not applicable to the jurisdiction of the Board of Railway Commissioners. That would not apply to that jurisdiction. I was referring to the remarks of the hon. member for

Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff), fur which he had good reason. But unless we are prepared to go the length of purchasing a line of steamships, then I say the difficulties are almost insurmountable unless all the other countries will come in. Even if they did come in, I see the other difficulty, it would suppress the tramp steamer. My hon. friend says they are doing business, and after all the tramp steamers enable us to get very cheap rates at times on special cargoes, and are often regulators of freight rates.
As to the guaranteeing, I am a firm believer in the opinion that we will soon have to do something in Canada to regulate our large mergers; but in this respect I shall make a confession. Owing to a difficulty that I seemed to have when I was a member of the Government in finding just what the Canadian Pacific Railway was earning on its railway and what the operation of -the road was costing, I was trying to study out some means by which I could have this company separated into two parts so that we could, in a clearer way, get at the real cost of the construction and operation of the railway. I had that in my mind, and I was wondering about it and had consulted one or two of my best advisers on railway matters as to how that could be brought about so that, once and for all, we could find out what would be a fair rate to impose on, the Canadian Pacific Railway in respect of rail freights. Now I find they are making this very separation, and I really think it is a good thing for the Dominion of Canada that we are getting the railway away from the steamship line. With the steamship separated from the railway I think we will be in a far better position to control rail rates.
Will the hon. gentleman explain to the committee how we will have better control of the railway when the steamship lines are separated?

It is hard to explain; but if my hon. friend had endeavoured to go into the earnings of the Canadian Pacific Railway when the steamships were so interminably mixed up with the railways that it was difficult to say just what part of the profits belonged to the railway and what part belonged to the steamships, he would realize the difficulty of arriving at a just conclusion as to the profits of the railway company.
That does not affect our control.

The control of the Board of Railway Commissioners or the extent to which they exercise it depends on what is a fair return to the railway company for its investment and operation; and if you cannot tell what the investment is or what the cost of operation is exactly, you cannot tell what is a proper rate to impose on the railway.
There is yet a question between the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Government as to whether the Government controls the Canadian Pacific rates by land at present. The Canadian Pacific Railway have never relinquished the right which they say exists under their original charter concerning rates.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Has my hon. friend seen the Order in Council passed on that subject?
I have not seen it, I was told such an order exists. My own opinion was that the Railway Board should control the rates.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: What has happened is this. The litigation between the Government and the company, initiated just before my hon. friend became Minister of Railways, was brought to a conclusion by an arrangement under which the Canadian Pacific Railway admitted that its rates were subject to the control of the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada. We withdrew the litigation on their express and explicit agreement, which is attached to the Order in Council, that henceforth the rates should be subject to the control of the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada. This agreement was made a year ago last November and there cannot be the slightest doubt that the Canadian Pacific Railway, in respect of its rates, is absolutely subject to the control of the Board of Railway Commissioners and has been ever since the 7th day of November, 1913. As a matter of fact, before that, by an informal agreement, the company had been assenting to the jurisdiction of the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada, as I am informed, but reserving, nevertheless, their right to raise the question if they saw fit to do so at any time.

The Order in Council had slipped my mind. I remember now that it was handed over to me on one occasion. The situation before the Order in Council was passed was that the Canadian Pacific Railway agreed tacitly to the control of the



rates, but reserved the right to raise the question under the old statute.
As to the guaranteeing of the bonds, the present is a very peculiar and exceptional time. Our securities, in common with all others, do not find such a ready sale at the present moment as we would wish. We are interested at the present moment very deeply in seeing that any securities that Canada has to offer through any of her great undertakings ought to be of the highest character and bring the highest price. This is not essentially a new organization at all, it is the separation of an old organization, which has a very high position, and rightly so, in this country into two integral parts, distinct and separate one from the other. The Canadian Pacific Railway, as I understand, are not asking permission to guarantee the bonds of some new organization in which to speculate in securities or of which the business will be speculative; they are simply asking that when they detach from the parent company the steamship line the parent company, which will still, in another way, own the child, may see it through by guaranteeing its securities.
