I think the situation is altogether different from what it would be if a new company were being organized and, a't the present moment, when it is essential not only to the company- but to the credit of Canada that the securities should be gilt-edged, I think no harm can be done by allowing the parent Canadian Pacific Railway Company to guarantee the bonds of its offspring, this new company, which really is part of itself. It is not an outside organization, it is not a new organization or company, but simply the old company dividing itself into two parts and asking that what is called the parent company may be allowed to look after the other company in the way of guaranteeing its bonds.
As to the position of the shareholders, I think the Prime Minister has stated that clearly. I might say in passing that the hon. member for South York (Mr. Maclean) will agree with me that the Canadian Pacific Railway never neglects its shareholders. The shareholders in the Canadian Pacific Railway Company proper will be part proprietors of every asset the Canadian Pacific Railway gets from the steamship company; and while the Canadian Pacific Railway will hand over to the other company the steamships, the steamship company will give them something in lieu of the steamships in which every shareholder will 
have a proprietary right as a stockholder in the original company. I am as anxious as any person can be for the control of freight rates, and will support any measure for that purpose that can be properly worked out. But this is something that will require international action, and cannot be successfully done otherwise.
As regards tne guaranteeing I see no reason why, under these peculiar conditions, I should not support the action of the committee in allowing the parent company to guarantee the assets of the company which is simply being detached.

My right hon. friend has made one thing clear at all events, and that is that the Canadian Pacific Railway, in going to Great Britain for incorporation, are not going where the regulations will be less strict. My right hon. friend has explained that the conditions are even more strict in many respects. We all know that no company likes to be under strict regulations; they much prefer lax regulations, and latitude to do what they want. Therefore this company has not been incorporated in Great Britain in order to be under less strict regulations. There must be some other reason, and I think that reason has been made very clear. They are anxious to escape from the control of this Parliament. They do not wish this Parliament or the Board of Railway Commissioners to control their freight rates. If that is not the case, they would never have incorporated the company in Great Britain, where the regulations are much stricter than here. I want to put a further point up to my right hon. friend. Suppose that the railway legislation introduced last year had become law.

If it was the law, it
would not touch this.

We shall see whether it would or not. Suppose it had become law last year. Under that legislation the Board of Railway Commissioners would have had the right to regulate the issues of securities by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. That is what the legislation is for. My hon. friend the Minister of Railways may shake his head, but if the legislation was not for that purpose why was it brought down?

It was for railroads,
not steamships.

My hon. friend seems
to forget that at that time as at present,

the steamboats were a part of the Railway Company.
No, they are not.

They are a part of the assets of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. The steamships are bought with the proceeds from stock authorized by this Government-if you do not choose to go further and say that they were partly bought with the cash, land and bonuses given to the Canadian Pacific railway. If that legislation had passed and become the law of the land, I am (Satisfied that, before issuing securities to raise money to buy further steamships for enlarging their fleet either on the Atlantic or on the Pacific, the Canadian Pacific Railway would have had to secure the (approval of the Board of Railway Commissioners. Apparently the Canadian Pacific. Railway see that very well. I have no doubt that, when the Prime Minister brought down the Railway Bill last year, they imagined he was anxious to have it passed; and although they believje that it will not be introduced this session, as my right hon. friend has stated that he did not intend to bring in any legislation this (Session except what was necessary in connection with the war, the Canadian Pacific evidently expect that at the next session of Parliament this legislation will be put on the statute books, and that by that legislation they would be prevented from doing what they proposed to do by this Bill. They believe that they would have to secure the approval of the Board of Railway Commissioners.
If the Government put this Bill through they must assume the responsibility. My right hon. friend further states that there is no likelihood of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company giving any part of the stock of the Canadian Pacific Ocean Services, Limited, as a bonus to the shareholders of Canadian Pacific stock, because in that case they might lose control of the steamship stock. But I would like to point out to my right hon. friend that they could give 49 per cent of that stock .as a bonus, and still retain control of the company. They could even give 75 per cent of it to the shareholders of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, .and still retain control for all practical purposes.
Another point was mentioned by the Minister of Railways, by the hon. member for Pictou, (and by the Prime Minister. They all presupposed that if tbs railway or 481
steamship company had to get the approval
of the Board of Railway Commissioners for an issue of stock or securities, or for their freight rates, the Commissioners would be unfair to them. I do not believe any hon. member of this House thinks anything of the kind. I think every member of this House believes, <and has a right to believe, that the Board of Railway Commissioners would be perfectly fair both to the railway and steamship company, and to the public of Canada. I think there is no force at all in that argument.
My hon. friend from South Renfrew (Mr. Graham} brought up another point in connection with earning the 10 per cent. My right hon. friend the Prime Minister states that that is now entirely eliminated, that the Canadian Pacific Railway by Order in Council are absolutely under the control of the Railway Commission so far as railway rates are concerned. But to my mind that is the very strongest argument why this Bill should not be passed. Because if, as was pointed out here to-day, the ocean carrying end is going to be the big profitable end, it would be quite possible for the Canadian Pacific Railway to give certain through freights, credit the small end to the railway company and the big end to the steamship company, and in that way avoid earning over 10 per cent on the railway line, which is under the control of the Railway Commissioners. They could make what profits they liked on the steamship end and we could say nothing about the matter.

Does the hon. gentleman not realize that the Board of Railway Commissioners would have control over the railway just as they have over the rates of any other railways, no matter whether a steamship service is at the end of the line or not. The Board of Railway Commissioners cannot allow the Canadian Pacific Railway to charge lower or higher freight rates than any other railway under the same conditions, whether there be a steamboat service at the end or not.

I realize that perfectly.
My hon. friend knows I am perfectly right. A railway and steamship company could keep their books to show as much profit as they liked on the steamship end, and as little as they liked on the railway end.

If the books were kept separate, would not the Railway Commission be able to ascertain much more easily whether there was any wrongdoing in connection with the bookkeeping, than if there

was one set of books for, say from Liverpool to Winnipeg or from Liverpool to Calgary? Would it not be easier for the commission if the books were kept separate? Would it not be an assistance to the Railway Commission if a Bill of this sort should pass? It struck me directly I saw the Bill that it would.

It would be if we had
control at both ends, but this whole legislation is for the purpose of evading any possible future control. I imagine that that is the object that the Canadian Pacific Railway have in view. I cannot see any other object. A railway company of the magnitude of the Canadian Pacific Railway comes . here and gives us as an excuse for this legislation that they are taking incorporation for the steamship end of their company in Great Britain where the conditions are much more onerous than they are here, as was pointed out by the Prime Minister, and they tell us that they are doing this to simplify book-keeping. Nobody takes that seriously. Nobody wouild imagine that the Canadian Pacific Railway would do that for the purpose of simplifying their bookkeeping. It is too absurd to be credited for one moment. There is something else behind it and as far as I have been able to judge by the debate, and by the character of the legislation before us, the only conceivable object is to have that end of their business withdrawn from any control by this Parliament through the board of Railway Commissioners in the future.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
In what way
does this withdraw it?

Because there is a question that we have not that power now. Under the legislation they have to come to this' Parliament for power to guarantee the bonds of this company and if we have not got the power then it is quite possible, we might get it. The legislation goes a long way to convince me that the Government thought we- had the power. If we have not we could get it. But if this legislation is passed it is out of our hands forever and we will not be able to get it. If tins legislation goes into force well and good, the Government, of course, will take the responsibility for it, but if my hon. friend was in earnest last year in' his proposed legislation I think in all fairness to the country and to the different railway and steamship companies this legislation ought to be held over until the legislation brought

down last session is dealt with by the House.

It has been said by the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) how well the company look after the interests of the shareholders. Certainly they do. Do they look after the interests of the public? What is happening to the public in this case? I want to call the right hon. the Prime Minister's attention to his argument that we are following tne procedure of the United States in compelling the companies here to dismember as they compel them to dismember in the United States.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I did not say
that we were compelling them to dismember.

No, but the point I
am making is that in the United States, when they were compelled to dissolve, they were compelled to cancel the capitalization. There is no reduction taking place in the capitalization of the Canadian Pacific Railway and no claim that there is. The same old capitalization continues and the same old argument will be made that we have taken the assets out and left the capitalization. They will come to the railway committee and say: We have to pay a ten per cent dividend on $225,000,000 or whatever their stock is. _ When the ex-minister says that his object was to keep them in order, did he try to have the capitalization that would be represented by the separation cancelled? No, the capitalization keeps to the same amount and if you wish to protect the public interest you ought to compel the company to cancel the capitalization. The hon. member for Renfrew is willing to allow the Canadian Pacific Railway to continue to do what it likes with its capitalization. Does he know that it made another recent issue of stock and sold that stock for less than it was worth to its own shareholders? Does he justify that? There has been so much of that in the past that the public demand the control and regulation of capitalization. They demanded it so strongly that the Government conceded it and put it in a Bill introduced last session. It ought to be made law this session when this Bill is going through. Certainly we should take that up next session, or we should take it up now so that these two matters might be dealt with concurrently.
Mr. SAM. SHARPE: It looks as if the Canadian Pacific Railway, by this legisla-

tion, is anticipating the railway Bill that it is proposed to bring down next session regulating the issue of securities by new companies, and the placing of these issues under the control of the Railway Board. The hon. Minister of Railways (Mr. Cochrane), the ex-Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham), and all the hon. members of this House who have supported this Bill, and who are against the amendment moved by my hon. friend from South York (Mr. Maclean), place their opposition to that amendment on something that does not exist in fact; my hon. friend does not pretend that the amendment will accomplish the control of ocean freight rates. He does not pretend that his amendment will have any control over ocean freight rates, but he says it will control the issue of securities by railway companies, the very object that the railway Bill will accomplish when it goes into force. Hon. members who have opposed the amendment of my hon. friend have not dealt with the question of capitalization and the effect of increasing the capitalization of the Canadian Pacific Railway and its subsidiary companies. Assuming that the capitalization of the Canadian Pacific Railway at the present time is $300,000,000, including the railway, the railway tracks, lands, hotels and steamship companies, if this Parliament allows them to separate their assets into several companies, leaving the railway with the parent company, the capitalization will still remain at $300,000,000, a subsidiary land company might be formed with a capitalization of $150,000,000, a steamship company with a capitalization of $40,000,000 and a hotel company with a capitalization of $10,000,000, which will increase the capitalization by $200,000,000; so that instead of a total capitalization of $300,000,000, the Canadian Pacific Railway will have a capitalization of $500,000,000, without airy increase in the value of the assets. That is what is going to happen under this legislation, and what my hon. friend from South York wants to do is exactly what is proposed to be done and there is the Bill which is promised next session. My hon. friend says: Do not press this Bill now before the House until next session, but if you do, put in this amendment so as to control the capitalization of the Canadian Pacific Railway. When this Bill was before the Railway Committee, the counsel of the Canadian Pacific Railway said that it was the intention that the stock in the subsidiary company was to be handed over to the Canadian Pacific Railway in return for the steamship. I asked
him if they intended to divide that among the shareholders or to retain it in bulk in the treasury of the Canadian Pacific Railway. He said that it would remain in bulk in the treasury of the Canadian Pacific Railway. When it was proposed that it should be kept in the treasury of the company instead of being divided among the shareholders in the form of a melon-cutting, they would not accept an amendment to that effect. It looks as if they were evading and anticipating the principle of the amendment which the Minister of Railways and Canals desires to apply to all the railway companies in the country, viz., that the securities issued by railway companies shall be under the control of the Railway Commissioners. We would all have confidence in the ability, fairness and integrity of the Railway Board in dealing with applications for the issue of securities. They are not going to impose any unfair conditions upon the Canadian Pacific Railway or any other company, but they will take into Consideration the circumstances in connection with each issue. The effect of this legislation will be to increase the capitalization of the Canadian Pacific Railway by $40,000,000 without increasing their assets one cent. It is not fair to the public who will have to pay rates, in addition to those now paid, sufficiently high to provide dividends for this increased capitalization.

I wish to move this amendment, of which I have given notice:
That the following clause be added to the Bill as clause N:
That the freight rates charged by the company shall be subject to the approval of the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada.
Amendment negatived.
Bill, reported.

That the said Bill be not now read the third time, but that it be recommitted to the Committee of the Whole for the purposes of amending the same by inserting the following:
5a. The said transfer or sale of the company's said steam or other vessels above authorized shall be subject to such terms and conditions as may be imposed by the Board of Railway Commissioners and the company shall not invest in or guarantee the securities of the said Canadian Pacific Ocean Services, Limited, or any other corporation to which it may sell or transfer its said vessels without the leave of said Board of Railway Commissioners first

had and obtained. And the Board may specify the purposes for which the proceeds arising from the sale or transfer of said boats by the Company may be used.
He said: I move this amendment for the reasons which I gave this afternoon in the committee.

Motion agreed to, and Bill read the third time and passed.
Bill No. 20, respecting the Canadian Northern Kailway Company-Mr. Bradbury-in committee.

The only amendment made to this Bill is that we have stricken out the words "or near" where they occur, so as to make it sure as to the places where the railway shall go. We have inserted after the word "company" in the second line of section 2, "subject to the restriction in the routes herein contained"-the restriction simply being that we struck out the words "or near" wherever they appear.
You are not making the road run like a rail fence?
the intention is to make it run to places and not only near to places.
I suppose the chairman of the Railway Committee will have no objection to inserting a provision that this road shall be started within six months, the same as in the former Bill.

I do not know that the conditions are the same. I said it a dozen times last session, and I said it two or three times this session, that where the change is made from two years to six months or any other period to commence the road, it is only done where a case has been made out for it. There was a good case made out to-day for limitation in a certain Bill. I want to say finally, and I hope people will understand me, that, so far as I am concerned, my understanding is that if the policy of the Railway Committee was changed last year it was not changed to any hard and fast rule as to time, but on the understanding that each Bill should be dealt with on its merits, and there is nothing inconsistent in making the period six months in one Bill and two years in another, if the facts justify it.

The railway from Strath-cona to Calgary is included in the Bill and there are ten miles oif that line built and graded and a bridge erected, but not an 
inch of steel has been laid. There has been no work done on it for four years, and the company is asking for an extension of time to five years in which to complete and two years in which to start work.
They have commenced part of it.

Yes, they have graded ten imiles and they have left it lying there for four years. There is more need for the six months' clause in this particular Bill than in any Bill I have known to come before this House.

Why?
M-r. DOUGLAS: The Canadian Northern is a live corporation. This proposed line will be in competition with the Calgary and Edmonton Railway, and it has been promised to the people for a long time. The company 'actually started operations and then suddenly stopped, and now they are asking for two years in which to recommence.

The Government are
partners in the Canadian Northern, they own 49 per cent of the stock, and I think they should set a good example and begin work within six months.

I went on record this afternoon about these extensions of time to railways, and I would point out that this 'company is asking power to complete a line and put it in operation within five years, but there is nothing in this Bill as to when they shall commence. The Bill says:
Unless the Canadian 'Northern Railway Company, hereinafter called the " company", completes and puts in operation within five years after the passing of this Act, the following lines of railway, all of which have been partly constructed, the powers of construction conferred upon the company by Parliament shall cease and he null and void, as respects so much of the said lines as then remains uncompleted.
There is included in this Bill a line from Calgary to Lethbridge. There has been some work done on that line, but I do not think anything was done during the past year. I would like to have some guarantee that this company shall recommence construction at once. Five years is altogether too long a period to give them to complete the road. When the end of the five years approaches, the company will probably start to do some work and then they will come back to Parliament and ask for a further extension of time, and put up the argument that they have done something. There ought to be some guarantee given to the House and to

the country as to when this company intends to start work on this line. The bonds on this particular line have been guaranteed by the province of Alberta. The province is anxious that construction should be commenced, and while I do not know the purport of the message the Premier of Alberta [DOT] sent to the Minister of Railways about it, I think he made the statement that the money had been raised and is in the bank, ready for the Canadian Northern the moment they undertake construction of this particular line.
You refer to that one piece of line?

Yes, I am speaking of the particular branch which affects my section of the country. I do not believe an extension of time over too long a period should be given to any company. I think there should be some guarantee given to Parliament that the construction of these lines should commence within at least a year, and especially the lines which have been guaranteed by provincial governments. This particular line, to which I am referring, was incorporated and the bonds guaranteed in 1909, and, although they have done some grading, I do not believe that any steel has yet been placed on any part of that road which has been under construction. While the financial conditions are bad this year, still there is money in the bank which the Canadian Northern can use in the construction of this particular line. I would like to have a statement from the Minister of Railways as to whether the Canadian Northern will be compelled to commence the construction of the lines, the bonds of which have been guaranteed by provincial governments.

If with respect to any line or branch line included in this Bill, the bonds of which have been guaranteed by the Provincial Government and sold and the money in the bank, the hon. gentleman moves an amendment to cut the time for commencement down to a year, I would be inclined to support him.
What proportion of the common stock of the Canadian Northern Railway Company does the Government now own?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: 40 per cent.

We have in this Bill a proposition from the Canadian Northern Railway Company to grant extension for five years to complete those branches that
were commenced over five years ago and that had a certain amount of work done on them. The settlers along those lines are patiently waiting every year for the work to be completed and nothing is being done. As the Government is now owner to the extent of 40 per cent in the Canadian Northern Railway Company, if it does not see that the company goes on and completes those branches, it will certainly have to assume 40 per cent of the condemnation of the settlers of those particular parts of the country. With the Government owning such a large proportion of that stock, it is its bounden duty to see that something is done. There is absolutely no excuse for any railway company grading two or three miles of road, as was done in my part of the country a few years ago, in order to prevent another road from coming in, and then as soon as the other road is shut off, stopping work for five or six years. As the Government is the junior member of the Canadian Northern to the extent of 40 per cent, it should see that that kind of work is discontinued in the future, or it will have to assume the responsibility for it.

In connection with the line to which I was referring, I am prepared to move an amendment that construction be commenced within a period of one year and that the line be completed and placed in operation within three years.
Is that part of the line guaranteed?

This line is guaranteed by the Alberta Government, and the Canadian Northern solicitor gave the Railway Committee the assurance that it was going on this year, so that this amendment will not counter their wishes.
Have the bonds been sold and is the money in the bank?
A certain proportion of the money is in the bank.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I have to declare this amendment out of order, because no notice has been given of it.
With the consent of the House it can be moved.
There is no objection to it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Mr. Buchanan moves an amendment:
That the following paragraph be added to clause (f) : always provided that the railway

If the House is unanimous, I am not objecting to this amendment, but I do not think that is the right way in which to bring about the amendment that the hon. gentleman wants. We have to look at the whole Bill. Section 2 reads:	-
Unless the Canadian Northern Railway Company, hereinafter called "The Company completes and puts in operation within five years after the passage of this Act the following lines of railway-
I think we would have to insert before (f) another section making what I have just said apply down as far as (f) and no farther, and then say that they may commence within one year and complete within five years this other railway. That is the proper way to make the legislation. Otherwise it will be very confusing, and it is not the usual way in which we pass such Bills.

I do not think the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Buchanan) will have any objection to the suggestion made by the Chairman of the Railway Committee. The amendment was drawn very hurriedly, and I am satisfied that in the way in which it was drawn it would be perfectly clear and intelligible because it is a rule of construction that an exception to a general clause always governs the general clause. It might, however, be better to arrange it as the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster) suggests; that is, section 2 would go down to the end of clause (e); then before (f) make a new section 3, which would read as follows:
Unless the Canadian Northern Railway Company, hereinafter called " the Company ", commences to construct within one year from the date thereof and completes and puts in operation within three years after the passing of this Act the following line of railway which is in course of construction, the powers of construction conferred upon the company by Parliament shall cease and be null and void as respects so much of the said line as remains uncompleted.
And then go on to (f). That might be more in accordance with the general policy of the drafting of the Bill. I am satisfied that the hon. member for Lethbridge will accept that suggestion.

Is the hon. gentleman of opinion that, we should mention here the time within which the line should be commenced?
[The Chairman.]
Yes, because work lias been suspended for two or three years.
But the line has been commenced.

They did some work in 1912 and probably some in 1913, but I am satisfied that nothing was done in 1914. They did do some grading a short distance out of the city of Calgary, but what I want to make sure of is that they will recommence construction.

Is it the intention of the Government to establish a rate of one cent upon letters between Ottawa and Hull? If not, why not?

Ottawa and Hull are
separate cities, and are, moreover, situated in different provinces. A drop letter is one that is posted and delivered in the same office and to have it otherwise would necessarily lead to an increase in the rate, as the department could not afford to carry letters from one office to another at a one-cent rate per ounce. If such were the case there would be no object in maintaining a two-cent rate per ounce for letters. If this privilege were given between Hull and Ottawa, it could not be withheld from all other places in Canada. To cairy letters in

Canada at the one-cent rate per ounce, in view of its long distances and sparse population, is not at present a possibility.

On the 2.3rd September, 1914, the departmental officers were instructed by the Postmaster General that as soon as the Lethbridge public building was ready for occupation it was the intention to appoint a new postmaster, and the Superintendent was requested to keep in touch with the progress made, and as soon as it was ready for the department to take possession to inform the Postmaster General so that the change could be made without delay.
